#833. Why Man Utd's Roma comeback has echoes of Mourinho and Solskjaer

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick (second left) hugs Shea Lacey after the 3-2 Champions League victory against Roma

It was impossible not to get swept up in the emotion and delirium of Manchester United's late 3-2 Champions League comeback win against Roma.

Old Trafford was transformed from a mutinous, baying cathedral of distrust and fury to one of joy and celebration.

Nine games and almost eight weeks is an eternity to wait for a victory at a club of Manchester United's size.

It didn't take Michael Carrick long to calm the mood.

"It's one win, so we're not getting too carried away with things, but it was an important win."

It was a huge result in the sense it bought Carrick some time. But given United's general state, no-one can be sure how much.

And, as was quickly pointed out in the aftermath of the victory, Manchester United have been here before.

Man Utd produce incredible second-half comeback to beat Roma

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?

Jose Mourinho (centre) was sacked after a 3-1 defeat at Liverpool in December 2018

'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'

As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.

As it turned out, the Mirror was wrong. Although United officials at the time tried to play down the situation, sources have since admitted the intention was to sack Mourinho after presiding over the club's worst start to a season in 29 years, and defeat by Newcastle would make it inevitable.

Much like the Roma game, the visitors raced into a two-goal lead and the atmosphere in the stadium started to turn, with most of the venom aimed at the director's box rather than the manager.

Mourinho, who had promoted Carrick to assistant coach, replaced Eric Bailly with Juan Mata after 19 minutes and it was Mata who scored the 70th-minute goal that sparked the comeback, completed by Alexis Sanchez in the final minute for a 3-2 victory.

After the game, Mourinho said the pressure on him was a "manhunt". However, the relationship between manager and club had been turning sour since the previous summer. His demand for Anthony Martial to be sold had been rejected, while record signing Paul Pogba was proving a problem.

While the Newcastle win sparked an improvement in form, a run of two wins in eight games culminating in a 3-1 loss at Liverpool led to Mourinho's dismissal 10 weeks later.

Former United defender Rio Ferdinand dismissed calls for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to be sacked before the Champions League encounter with Atalanta on 20 October 2021 as representative of "current fan culture".

Carrick was also part of Solskjaer's coaching group as United went top of the Premier League when they beat Newcastle just over a month earlier, but two wins in seven suggested all was not well.

As he did with Roma, coach Gian Piero Gasperini saw his team establish a two-goal lead by half-time, then collapse. Cristiano Ronaldo was the matchwinner on this occasion, nine minutes from time for another 3-2 win.

Even if United had lost that night, it is hard to think Solskjaer's job would have been under threat. What followed immediately afterwards was a totally different story.

Liverpool came to Old Trafford and established a four-goal first-half lead. Jurgen Klopp's men won 5-0, their biggest ever away win over their old rivals.

Many United fans thought Solskjaer should go that night. It was three weeks later that it happened, after a 4-1 defeat at Watford.

Man Utd beat Roma - the other great Champions League comebacks

Fernandes critical of media 'lies' about Carrick relationship

Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes celebrates Matheus Cunha's winner against Roma

One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.

If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.

United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.

The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.

When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.

In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.

Victory against Villa, albeit with Â£70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December.

Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November.

"It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.

There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

#832. Craig Melvin Confronts Martha Stewart After Halloween Controversy

Martha Stewart and Craig Melvin reunited on Today so the lifestyle guru could express her regrets for blaming the host for her “stupid” decision to dress like a homeless person on Halloween.

Martha Stewart is serving up some more accountability for her actions.

After the Martha Stewart Living founder blamed Craig Melvin for her dressing as a homeless person for Halloween, claiming that her decision came from the Today anchor accidentally spilling chocolate on her during the Oct. 30 episode, she addressed those comments with the veteran journalist.

"It was Saturday, and it was Halloween, and I was invited to a party," Stewart recalled to Melvin on the Nov. 6 episode of the morning show. "I was very busy all day doing a lot of gardening. We're planting lots of trees up at the farm, and I really hadn't planned a Halloween costume this year."

Though she emphasized that she usually does very "elaborate costumes," she said she "didn't have a costume" because Melvin—who was dressed as her BFF Snoop Dogg for Today's beloved Halloween episode—dropped chocolate ganache on her white sweater as they learned to decorate a themed cheesecake.

"I don't blame you at all," Stewart asserted. "It was a joke that I said I blamed you. It was stupid. It was tone deaf."

Meanwhile, Melvin was ready for clarification on his alleged role in this mess.

"I was making a joke," the lifestyle guru emphasized. "I was giving a talk, and I just made a joke that you had spilled chocolate on me, and so I couldn't wear that costume, which I had planned to wear on Halloween night to this party."

Even so, Melvin made sure to emphasize that he had no involvement in Stewart's costume controversy.

He added, "To be clear, there was no connection between that and the costume later."

As for what lessons the 85-year-old learned?

"Pay closer attention to social issues," she reflected. "I'm aware of all those social issues, as you can imagine, and I care desperately about all the problems facing us, but I made a mistake. I was stupid. What else can I say?"

"I'm so sorry," she continued. "I hope that my followers and my fans and the rest of America forgive me for doing something that was not meant in any way to be a bad thing."

But it wasn't just online critics slamming Stewart's costume. In fact, she admitted her 14-year-old grandson Truman told her it was "tone deaf" after she sent him a photo of the look.

"I apologized because I was not making fun of anybody or making light of the great problems that face our country," she added. "I certainly hope our new administration takes big steps to repair a lot of the damage that's being done, and the poor and the hungry and everyone else is taken care of better."

Before suggesting Melvin was behind her costume, Stewart expressed remorse and asserted that the homelessness issue in the U.S. is close to her heart.

"Homelessness continues to remain one of America's greatest challenges and ongoing crises," she said in a separate statement to People on Nov. 1, "something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic."

Before the debacle, however, she and Melvin had a spooktacular time on Today's Halloween episode. Keep reading to see the costumes worn by the other cohosts.

#831. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Bart Verbruggen (Brighton): He was unreal. Lots of saves which kept Brighton in it at Manchester City, even the last-ditch stop where it hit him in the face.

Just an impenetrable wall. Brighton should really have lost by two or three goals, but Verbruggen was the reason they managed to hold on for a 1-0 win.

Archie Gray (Tottenham): I'm going with a fully north London back four. Gray scored and defended really well against Crystal Palace. He was under a lot of pressure when Tottenham were in bad form and got a lot of stick, but now Spurs are starting to pick up I'm going to give him a bit of credit.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): He was a beast in Arsenal's 1-0 win at Anfield. Head it, kick it, throw your body in front of the ball. He defended and fought for the team, getting the job done.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham): Van Hecke got a goal and he's really growing into his role at Spurs. I still think he was a little bit overpriced, but all in all he's had a solid start, coming up with a few goals. Micky van de Ven next to him gives him confidence that he can go and be really aggressive, because Van der Ven will cover him with his pace.

Jurrien Timber (Arsenal): Timber got away with a shirt pull on Alexander Isak and I'm really surprised the referee and video assistant referee (VAR) didn't look at it. But I thought he recovered and defended really well at full-back.

Romeo Lavia (Chelsea): I thought Lavia was excellent for Chelsea. People will turn to Manchester United having 10 men, but the 60 minutes before that Chelsea were all over the place. Lavia was the only constant breaking up play, keeping the ball moving. Plus he had an assist.

Declan Rice (Arsenal): A proper captain's performance, he gets the job done all over the pitch. He got a little assist for himself, too.

Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry): Sakamoto goes unnoticed by a lot of people, but I think he works really hard for the team and he is very humble in his approach. On Saturday he also delivered in a massive win for his team against Sunderland.

Johan Manzambi (Aston Villa): Another assist for the 21-year-old who is just flying. His confidence is through the roof and he is taking over this Villa team. Really good player, only going to get better. He was taken off thinking about the Champions League game against Barcelona, but up until that point Fulham couldn't really stop him.

Ollie McBurnie (Hull): Grafter, scrappy, endeavour, goals, assists... he had it all in his game in the draw against Ipswich.

He epitomises what Hull are: a player that's always overlooked, a team that's always overlooked, but they've got some spirit and some fight.

Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry): Unbelievable solo goal. It's really good to see the big fella back playing and being in a situation where he can impose himself. If Coventry are to stay up, he's going to be why.

Frank Lampard (Coventry): He has been really good. Coventry have taken care of business against Sunderland, it was a massive six-pointer and his team came out front-footed, aggressive and also did a job on a very good Sunderland team.

Also a massive nod to Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta for getting the job done at Liverpool.

#830. Nations championship, Rugby League World Cup and NFL action – follow with us

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

There will be plenty to talk about in the world of football on Saturday morning. As well as building up to Saturday’s four Premier League games, David Tindall will be looking at the fallout from Frank Lampard’s return to Everton with Coventry on Friday night and reaction to Thomas Tuchel’s last England squad of the year. But it’s also FA Cup first round proper day, when League One and League Two sides find themselves pitched against other lower-division sides or at risk of being giantkilled by non-league clubs. There’s also a Savage occasion on Saturday night at London Road, when Robbie’s Peterborough take on the Reading side for whom his son Charlie plays. Send your thoughts on all the issues to matchday.live@theguardian.com, and let us know if you are off to one of those Cup ties.

It’s very tight in the Premier League’s mid-table, with three teams on 12 points and four on 11 occupying the places between eighth and 14th before this round of matches. One of the latter category host one of the former on Saturday, with Daniel Farke and Roberto De Zerbi fairly happy with their positions right now but aware that Leeds and Tottenham both need to push on if they are to stay properly clear of relegation talk and instead push claims for places in Europe. Scott Murray is your live host, while Aaron Bower reports from Elland Road.

North and south/east are meeting all this weekend as the second half of the inaugural Nations Championship builds towards its climax at Twickenham on the last weekend of the month, and the All Blacks’ trip to Murrayfield is the pick of the day’s matches. Scotland have still never beaten New Zealand, and the worry for Gregor Townsend’s team is that after some severe stumbles the visitors are back on firm footing. Daniel Gallan is your guide minute by minute, while Michael Aylwin is in Edinburgh.

There are two 3pm kick-offs in the Premier League, with Arsenal hosting Hull and Newcastle at Fulham, and Barry Glendenning will have all the news from the leaders’ meeting with the playoff winners and a meeting of the dissatisfied at Craven Cottage. In the FA Cup first round, we will be on the lookout for shocks. Perhaps there will be one at Boreham Wood, where the runaway leaders of the National League are at home to the 2013 winners, Wigan. There are also some all non-league ties, including the phoenix club Salisbury FC of National League South at home to Sholing of the Southern League Premier and Dover, another National League South side, hosting Wealdstone, one step higher. If you are at any of the ties, let Barry know what’s going on.

Oliver Glasner’s move to Forest has not gone smoothly, as evidenced by his anguished comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford that “I don’t need to be liked. I’m not here to be liked. I’m here to bring success to this club.” Manchester City aren’t winning popularity contests at present, either, and have lost a couple of football matches, too, after their steamroller start – if Arsenal have beaten Hull in their afternoon game, then the visitors to the City Ground will kick off six points off the top. Tom Bassam will follow events live, while Jonathan Wilson reports.

After sealing the title in Mexico City last weekend to become the youngest ever F1 champion, Kimi Antonelli aged 20 and (almost) a quarter is back in action, as Mercedes seek to close out a first constructors’ title since 2021 and the rest of the grid try to maximise their finishing places over the next four rounds. Estimates say each place in the team standings is worth about £7m. Ferrari should take second place, holding a 122-point advantage over Red Bull, but the squabbles between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc aren’t helping, while it is still fairly close between Red Bull and McLaren in the battle for third. Join Philip Cornwall for qualifying live, while Giles Richards reports.

It’s a double-header in Sydney, as the Jillaroos take on Fiji in the women’s tournament before the Kangaroos face Samoa, as the World Cup hosts aim for places in the following Sunday’s Brisbane finals. Angus Fontaine is on minute-by-minute for the women’s match, while Jonathan Howcroft looks after the men’s, and Jack Snape reports on both.

It’s another bumper Sunday of Premier League action and Emillia Hawkins, Simon Burnton and Tim de Lisle will have all the buildup to the games as well as picking over Saturday’s action. Depending on results, a manager or two could be brushing up his CV. Talking of which, there will be news in advance of the match at Old Trafford, pitting Manchester United’s current manager, Michael Carrick, against someone tipped to be his successor, Unai Emery of Aston Villa. Email matchday.live@theguardian.com with your views

A week after the men’s team won at Anfield, Arsenal’s women arrive badly in need of victory: the once all-conquering Gunners are only in the top half on goal difference, thanks to Alessia Russo’s late equaliser against Aston Villa last Sunday. Liverpool are in 11th but with the same goal difference (minus one) and only two points fewer, but after last week’s 4-1 defeat at West Ham they have won only one of their last seven. Emillia Hawkins has the live blog while Tom Garry reports.

Before that game at Old Trafford, the Europa/Conference League rearrangements mean Brighton v Brentford, Crystal Palace v Liverpool, Sunderland v Chelsea and Ipswich v Bournemouth are all at 2pm. Simon Burnton will be going around the grounds, seeing if Brighton can hang on to the leaders’ coattails; if one of Liverpool and Palace can manage a win after three defeats and a draw between them across four matches in the previous week; if struggling Sunderland can get a much-needed win against Chelsea; and if Ipswich can maintain their mid-table status against the Europa League’s all-conquering Bournemouth.

With finals weekend of the inaugural Nations Championship coming up at the end of the month, England would love to be back at Twickenham on the Sunday, you would imagine, when the top team in the north plays the top team from the south. What, though, if Steve Borthwick’s side lose to Australia? They might still get a Sunday match – but in the fourth v fourth warm-up against, say, France or South Africa. England need a clean sweep and South Africa to beat France next weekend in order to make the grand finale, and Daniel Gallan will take you through their efforts live while Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher report from south-west London.

It’s the last Premier League game before an international break that could open up the managerial merry-go-round, despite being the old-style two-weeker rather than the three-week one that straddled September and October. Michael Carrick will be trying to build on Manchester United’s thrilling comeback against Roma, while Unai Emery will hope Aston Villa can respond to his latest defeat at the Camp Nou. Tim de Lisle will have all the live updates, while Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin report from Old Trafford.

It’s so nice they named it thrice: the grand prix venue can be referred to as the city of São Paulo; as the Autódromo José Carlos Pace; or perhaps most famously by the neighbourhood it sits in, Interlagos. If it wasn’t for that pesky kid, then this could be a title race for the ages: Max Verstappen is two points ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who is nine ahead of George Russell, with Charles Leclerc five more back. And even Lando Norris is within a win of Leclerc, and has twice as many race victories as the Monégasque and Hamilton. Daniel Harris is on the live blog, while Giles Richards reports.

It’s week nine, no one can go unbeaten now, and Graham Searles will have news of the crop of 1pm eastern, 6pm GMT kick-offs. They include the meeting of two table-toppers, though it’s fair to say the AFC West’s 6-and-2 Broncos are in better shape than the NFC South’s 3-and-4 Panthers, who are hosts. Other matches include the Jets at the Chiefs and the Lions at the Dolphins. Graham will also have news of the 9.30am eastern/2.30pm game between Atlanta and Cincinnati, the NFL’s first visit to Madrid.

#828. Meghan Markle's Dad Thomas Markle Arrested in Child Pornography Case

Thomas Markle Sr., the father of Meghan Markle, was arrested by the FBI on Nov. 6 in Florida on suspicion of possessing child sex abuse materials. He previously denied the allegations.

The investigation into Thomas Markle is coming to a head.

The father of Meghan Markle was arrested on Nov. 6 by the FBI in Florida on suspicion of possessing child sex abuse materials, the U.S. Attorney's Office confirmed in a release. He is expected to make his first appearance in court the same day.

According to the statement shared online, Thomas allegedly possessed materials which included "sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls," in two storage units he rented in the Los Angeles area since 2008. He’s been charged with one count of possession of child pornography. If convicted, per the statement, Thomas would face a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

“Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayl. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

The 82-year-old’s arrest reportedly occurred at the Florida care home he’d been living in since he underwent a leg amputation in December 2025, per the The Sun, citing footage obtained at the scene. A wheelchair-bound Thomas could be seen in handcuffs in photos published by the outlet.

E! News has attempted to locate a rep or attorney for Thomas for comment but was unable to do so.

Thomas’ arrest comes mere weeks after his son Thomas Markle Jr., Meghan’s half-brother, accused their father of possessing child sex abuse materials, which he said he found in his house in the Philippines.

Thomas, however, soon denied all the allegations.

“I'm shocked, I'm hurt and I'm very upset that my son is making these accusations against me,” he told The Daily Mail on Oct. 23. “I could never do what I'm being accused of. It's the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

He added, “This is bulls--t. It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

His daughter Samantha Markle, who has been his caretaker in Florida, also slammed the allegations.

“There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up,” Samantha added to the outlet. “He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”

At the time, the FBI confirmed its involvement in the investigation into Thomas, noting it would “provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”

As for Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex—who shares two children with husband Prince Harry—shared she was “deeply distressed” over the allegations in a statement with E! News, noting her thoughts were with “any children who may have been harmed.”

The 45-year-old also shared insight into what information she’d been made privy to previously.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection,” she explained. “That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”

Though she didn’t specify he allegations, she noted they’re a large reason she’s been estranged from Thomas in recent years.

“I hope it can now be understood that despite certain media publications' distortion over the years,” she said, “any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.”

As for now, she hopes justice can be served.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” Meghan concluded. “The priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

(E! and MS NOW are both part of Versant Media family.)

#827. Football Daily | You want proper football? Here are the FA Cup first-round ties to look out for

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

For the FA Cup, the early rounds are the juice. The first round proper to be played out over the long weekend is looking, well, proper. And on Saturday at 3pm GMT, a proper time, 31 ties will kick off. No VAR, either. At the stage when the bottom two Football League divisions join the competition, focus remains on those non-league clubs fighting for the honour of the pyramid …

Mansfield v Macclesfield In January, Macclesfield achieved the greatest shock in the competition’s history, knocking out the holders, Crystal Palace, in the third round. John Rooney’s National League North team head through the Pennines to face soundalikes Mansfield. Those from Macclesfield often find themselves having to correct others on coming from the Cheshire town rather than the one in Nottinghamshire. Macclesfield are such a modern club these days they have a sporting director in Keith Curle, a former Stags manager. Curle and current Mansfield boss Nigel Clough were England teammates at Euro 92, of which the less said the better.

Bradford City v Marine Merseyside’s most authentic, proper football club? Neither Everton nor Liverpool can compete with Crosby’s Marine. When modern football gets too much, the temptation to savour a pie and pint at Rossett Park, the club of Roly Howard, legendary manager for 33 years, becomes strong. On Saturday, Marine travel to Bradford City, on something of a slide since Graham Alexander de-camped to manage Preston.

Burton v AFC Rushden & Diamonds Fans at Burton’s Pirelli Stadium will see Billy Sharp’s comeback at 76. One of the Football League’s very top marksmen, the Championship’s all-time scorer on 130 recently retired but has returned with AFC Rushden & Diamonds, the phoenix club of a former temporary employer for whom he scored his first goal when loaned there in 2005, before they were liquidated six years later. A striker who defines the term “well-travelled” – including a spell at LA Galaxy – blink and you will miss Sharp, as the prodigal return is for one game only, in search of his 300th career goal. He departed Doncaster on the tantalising total of 299.

Plymouth Argyle v Alvechurch Alvechurch, representing a Worcestershire village, was previously most famous for giving the world Alan “Smudger” Smith (incidentally another member of that Euro 92 squad). The less said about his substitution for old pal Gary Lineker against Sweden the better. Smith’s alma mater, in the Southern League, travel to Plymouth Argyle, led by Tom Cleverley, the former brand turned aspirant tracksuit manager. Two seasons ago the Pilgrims’ progress down to League One was offset by beating eventual Premier League champions Liverpool in the third round. Should that fall flat, the city gets another helping on Monday night when Parkway take on Berkhamsted, the commuter town’s community club.

Cray Wanderers v Stockport County Representing the Isthmian League are Cray Wanderers, who claim to be London’s oldest football club, whose origins are traced to 1860, older perhaps than even Notts County. Playing in Chislehurst, best known for its caves, “The Wands” take on high-flying League One Stockport County, led by The Wire’s Jimmy McNulty.

Peterborough v Reading All that and a Savage family reunion as the Posh, managed by Robbie, host son Charlie’s team, the Royals. The Cup properly runneth over.

“It’s an incredible achievement for the family and the brothers to both be nominated for the national team. He’s more defensive than Jude” – Thomas Tuchel talks about his decision to call up Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, with the ability to bolt the door shut behind his rampaging elder sibling quite possibly a big factor.

Join Scott Murray at 8pm GMT for red-hot minute-by-minute updates of Everton 0-0 Coventry in the Premier League.

double quotation markJohn Aloisi winning or choking​ the Chinese Super League, a league so ‘super’ that nine of all 16 clubs in it started the season on negative points due to ‘match-fixing, gambling and corruption’ by the way, and the league leaders not even scoring a single goal in seven hours, is really not something to lay upon someone with a bad hangover. Apropos of nothing, if anyone has any objections to my views on the Chinese Super League, please address any correspondence to: Mr K Mbappé, Madrid (there’s no point two of us getting into trouble)” – Noble Francis.

In late 1991 I was working in the Patents Advice Centre, Newcastle Central Library. A gentleman asked for help to possibly patent an ‘invention’: a football shirt with the seams held together by Velcro, so that any tug would ‘open’ the seam and provide clear evidence to the referee of illegal cloth gathering. As I helped him search for possible equivalent innovations in our paper database (yes kids!) we chatted amiably until I asked how he had come to this seemingly simple yet brilliant innovation. #826. Meet the people set for key role in deciding Man City fate

Manchester City have been sponsored by Etihad since May 2009

They are the five individuals at the Premier League set to play a key role in the fate of Manchester City.

The competition's board has the responsibility of recommending a punishment after the seismic news in September of the club being found guilty of breaching financial rules by an independent commission.

While that three-person commission panel will ultimately decide on a sanction, the Premier League's submission will be considered, along with the view of City of course, who maintain their innocence and have appealed.

It is not known when a sanction hearing will take place, nor what sanction the Premier League will want for what it describes as the most significant disciplinary case in its history, with a fine, points deduction, expulsion or the stripping of past titles all possible.

So who makes up the Premier League's board, and how have their recommendations over punishments been received in past disciplinary cases?

Among various roles and responsibilities, the board is the entity responsible for prosecuting breaches of Premier League rules.

It comprises the league's chair, chief executive, and three independent non-executive directors, with no club representatives included - in order to provide independence and neutrality.

Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

Alison Brittain has kept a low profile since becoming the league's first female chair almost four years ago. Formerly a senior executive in the hospitality and financial services sectors, she is also chair and trustee of The King's Trust Group.

Described as "sensible" by one acquaintance, in September she spoke at a university event, revealing that she was initially sceptical about joining the Premier League because she had never worked in sport.

Two senior club executives - the former Arsenal CEO Vinai Venkatesham (now at Spurs), and ex-Aston Villa CEO Christian Purslow - told her that her skillset was what the league needed, helping to persuade her to apply.

She said: "They actually spent some time talking to me and saying 'we aren't looking for a super fan. In fact we're looking for the exact opposite - somebody who will bring a different mindset. A business mindset, governance standards, be able to reset us a little bit into a different way'â¦and so I then went through the process and ended up in the job."

Describing herself as a "lifelong Manchester United fan [who] stood in the Stretford End before it had seats, as a kid" because of her family's allegiance, Brittain is now also a Brentford supporter. In 2025, she received unanimous backing from the 20 clubs to continue for a second three-year stint.

Speaking in 2024, Brittain acknowledged the league was "not without its challenges". But she has hailed what she describes as "the most exciting competition in the world", and its global appeal, calling it an "enormous soft power asset" for the country.

She also recently said that "the whole point of running the league... is to make sure the competitive balance stays really good. Because what makes us successful is this virtuous circle of anyone could win any match any dayâ¦ there has to be jeopardy."

She added: "Someone has to care about keeping that balance, because if you ask the clubs they'd rather not have that balance because they'd like to win all the time."

When asked if that was her job, she replied: "Absolutely. That's my job."

According to Purslow, Brittain has "extremely good people skills and diplomacy in a role where keeping 20 owners more or less happy is not an easy job. She is a very down to earth, straightforward person, and that plays well."

Richard Masters has been the Premier League's chief executive since 2019

The league's chief executive since 2019, Richard Masters is a much more familiar face to football fans.

When the independent commission's 'core decision' on City was announced in September, he said it "vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case", and that the league has "a key responsibilityâ¦ to ensure that the rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition".

He added that it was "paramount that the league remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously."

Masters said: "There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans."

Reportedly having grown up an Aston Villa fan, in 2024 Masters assured a parliamentary committee that "the Premier League board applies the rules consistently, irrespective of the club in question".

The board is completed with three other directors:

Mai Fyfield - a former Sky executive who during her 20-year career at the company led its bidding for three Premier League TV cycles, and currently sits on the board of BBC Commercial.

Dharmash Mistry - a technology venture capitalist and entrepreneur who also has experience of working with the BBC as a former non-executive director at the corporation. Mistry is "smart and theoretical" according to one colleague. He chairs the Premier League's audit and finance committee and is its representative on the FA's board.

Matthew Ryder - a senior barrister, part-time judge and a former deputy mayor of London when he had responsibility for social mobility and social engagement. He is also a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian newspaper, alongside other non-executive roles. Describing himself as "a longstanding and passionate football fan", he also chairs the league's legal advisory group. He told a conference last year that his membership of the Premier League board had been "deeply rewarding... it's a fascinating time to be in football."

BBC Sport has approached the board members via the Premier League, but it declined to comment.

How did Man City's 'disguised funding scheme' work?

The Manchester City case is unique in its scale, and so it is uncertain how relevant previous cases are when looking at the kind of sanctions the Premier League has recommended. But it is clear that independent commissions do not necessarily agree with the Premier League's board when it comes to clubs' potential punishments.

In 2023, the league argued for a 12-point sanction for Everton after the club breached financial rules, with a commission then settling on a 10-point punishment instead, which was reduced to six points on appeal.

In 2024, the Premier League suggested that Nottingham Forest should be docked eight points over a larger PSR overspend, but the commission again disagreed, settling on a four-point punishment.

This year the Premier League argued that an appropriate sanction for Leicester City - for an overspend in 2023-24 - was a 12-point deduction to be applied in the Championship. The independent commission instead recommended that a six-point deduction be imposed by the EFL.

There is also an alternative to contested proceedings.

Earlier this year the Premier League board reached a 'sanctions agreement' with Chelsea which resulted in a Â£10m fine and suspended transfer ban after admitting making Â£47m in secret payments to unregistered agents and third parties over transfers between 2011 and 2018.

The league said: "When considering the appropriate sanction, the board noted that the club's proactive self-reporting, admissions of breach and exceptional co-operation throughout the investigation acted as significant mitigating factors."

Who is Rui Pinto? Is he a whistleblower or hacker? The BBC finds out more about the man responsible for bringing chaos to the world of football over the last decade.

#825. Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results

German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead Israel's new government.

Although the right-wing bloc, including religious hardliners, led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset.

Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult.

Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin.

But he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.

"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.

In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.

"The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end," she said.

All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.

Relations between Germany and Israel are traditionally close, in part because of Germany's historical responsibility for Nazi Germany's murder of millions of Jews during the Holocaust.

Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.

Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians.

In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after Israel's 2026 election.

So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.

At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremists, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people, and above all the elected politicians, will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."

The Arab-majority parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel made large gains in this election. They are usually classified as part of the current opposition camp. The historic results by these parties could lead them to play a kingmaker role in coalition formation.

However, Netanyahu’s bloc have ruled out working with the Arab-majority parties.

Eisenkot's opposition bloc has not yet said whether it would be willing to form such a coalition, but one of the Arab-majority parties, United Arab List/Ra'am, featured a Jewish candidate, and has stated its willingness to work with Eisenkot’s bloc to unseat Netanyahu.

Hardt believes a minority government led by Eisenkot and supported by parties representing Arab Israelis is conceivable.

"The major campaign carried out by Netanyahu's camp, aimed primarily against Arab Israelis, greatly mobilized the opposition, to the point where his camp no longer has a majority."

The vice president of the German Bundestag, Green Party politician Omid Nouripour, told DW: "Frankly, after all the turmoil that has occurred — for example, regarding judicial reform — this is good news for Israeli democracy."

This article was originally published in German.

#824. Cape Verde captain Ryan Mendes cleared of rape allegation as woman charged with false statement

New Zealand police dismiss claim of sexual assault at Auckland hotel

Incident alleged to have occurred after football friendly in March

New Zealand police have dismissed a rape allegation against Cape Verde football captain Ryan Mendes and have charged the accuser with making a false statement.

Detective inspector Scott Beard said Friday the claim that a sexual assault occurred at a central Auckland hotel in March had not been substantiated.

A 40-year-old woman has been charged under New Zealand’s Crimes Act with making a false statement. She is expected to appear in court next week.

“A decision to prosecute in these circumstances is not taken lightly and follows months of investigative work by our Adult Sexual Assault Team,” Beard said.

The incident was alleged to have occurred hours after Cape Verde played Chile in a friendly match in Auckland, won 4-2 by Chile.

Mendes’ lawyer, Karl Trotter, said the allegation resulted in his client facing intense international media speculation.

Cape Verde qualified for the 2026 World Cup and the subject of the alleged assault arose at almost every media conference Mendes attended.

“Mr Mendes was thrilled to finally be able to get this behind him and he regards it as a complete vindication,” Karl Trotter told the New Zealand Herald newspaper.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“It is to be hoped that this recent turn of events, clearing Mr Mendes of the allegation of rape, attracts the same level of media attention as the original reporting.”

The 36-year-old Mendes is Cape Verde’s most capped player, having made 103 appearances since his debut in 2010. He currently plays for RS Berkane in Morocco.

#821. America Ferrera Reveals What She Knows About Barbie 2

As the deal for the sequel to Greta Gerwig’s Barbie movie up in the air, star America Ferrera revealed what she knows about the film in an exclusive E! News interview for The Cat in the Hat.

America Ferrera is a Barbie girl, but she knows nothing about the Barbie 2 world.

While the sequel for Greta Gerwig’s film inspired by the Mattel toy and starring Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling has been up in the air for years, Ferrera admitted that she’s just Ken, er, Gloria—and doesn’t have any update.

“I don’t know anything about Barbie 2,” Ferrera admitted in an exclusive E! News interview for The Cat in the Hat alongside costar Paula Pell. “I don’t have to pretend like I don’t know anything because I actually don’t know anything.”

Ferrera’s update comes as speculation swirls around the possibility for a follow-up to the 2023 film, with reports earlier this year noting that the movie could be shelved due to ongoing salary negotiations between Warner Bros. and the original film’s cast.

Meanwhile, Ferrera—mom to Sebastian, 8, and Lucia, 6, with husband Ryan Piers Williams—is excited about bringing another iconic character to life, starring as mom Carmen in the Bill Hader-led film.

“The Cat in the Hat is so iconic,” the Ugly Betty alum mused. “I grew up loving Dr. Seuss books and I have two littles and I’ve read The Cat in the Hat to them a ton. Actually, my favorite part of the book was always the very last line of the book which was, ‘What would you do if your mother asked you?’ And I’d always turn to my kids and be like, ‘Would you tell me the truth?’”

Fast forward to this opportunity, Ferrera admitted it felt as easy as counting one fish, two fish, red fish, blue fish to take the role.

“Getting to say to my kids I’m going to be the voice of the mom in The Cat in the Hat, I did it for them,” she mused. “But a little bit for me.”

And Ferrera’s kids already gave her a glowing review for the film, also starring Quinta Brunson and Bowen Yang, which officially hits theaters today, Nov. 6.

“We saw it yesterday,” she revealed. “We had the best time. They loved it. It was really sweet.”

Of course, Ferrera isn’t so sure her kids would, in fact, tell her if The Cat in the Hat came for a visit.

“I can’t tell if it gave me cool mom points or if they’re like, ‘Ugh, mom that’s you,’” she joked. “Because I am such a mom in this, too, where they were like, ‘We’ve heard the same things.’”

While Barbie 2 still remains uncertain, keep reading for secrets about the original film…

Margot Robbie, who stars as Barbie and also produced the film, admitted that she always wanted Ryan Gosling to be her Ken. She said he was written into the script—as the character "Ken Ryan Gosling"—and joked, "We pretty much wouldn't take no for an answer."

Writer-director Greta Gerwig had her back too. "We just kept bothering you," she said to to Ryan in an SXM interview. "Margot was like, 'Is it weird if I go to his house?' I was like, 'Don't go to his house. We're just gonna stay put.' Send a follow-up text."

As Margot teased, "I would see a sea of blue on my phone."

Margot gave Ryan daily gifts inspired by his character Beach Ken.

"She left a pink present with a pink bow, from Barbie to Ken, every day while we were filming," Ryan told Vogue. "They were all beach-related. Like puka shells, or a sign that says 'Pray for surf.'"

He said that he's "never quite figured out" what Ken's job as "Beach" means, "But I felt like she was trying to help Ken understand, through these gifts that she was giving."

"I think we said it was scheduling conflict, that's what we said," Amy Schumer said on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen in June 2023. "But yeah, it really was just, like, creative differences. But you know what? There's, like, a new team behind it, and it looks like it's very feminist and cool. So, I will be seeing that movie."

These Barbies were almost movie stars—or, rather, these movie stars were almost Barbies. After Amy left the movie, Anne Hathaway was signed up to take the lead, but it was later reported that she was no longer involved. When Margot got on board, she tried to recruit Gal Gadot to join as another Barbie, but the Wonder Woman star wasn't available.

Greta's former Lady Bird and Little Women muse Saoirse Ronan was also set to appear in the film but had to cancel. "I was supposed to do a cameo because I live in London and they were [filming] there," the actress admitted to People. "There was a whole character I was going to play—another Barbie. I was gutted I couldn't do it."

"We've always tried to get in a proper fart joke and we've never done it," Greta told IndieWire. "We had like a fart opera in the middle [of Barbie]. I thought it was really funny... And that was not the consensus."

But her editor Nick Houy has hope she'll let one rip in a future film: "We need to work it into a more significant narrative moment next time."

While the script comedically name-drops other shows and movies—like the The Godfather, Pride and Prejudice and Zack Snyder's Justice League—there are multiple Easter eggs to The Wizard of Oz hidden in the set. A movie theater marquee shows that the 1939 film is playing in the doll world, but the inspiration didn't stop there.

"[The Wizard of Oz] does something that I wanted to emulate," Greta said in an interview, "which it's using these incredible sound stages and these painted skies and this sense of 'authentic artificial,' which I think is very beautiful and emotional."

The 39-year-old explained, "I think of the painted backdrop of the Emerald City as they go towards it, and we put in our movie, we have the pink brick road, instead of the yellow brick road. We also have beautiful painted backdrops of horizons. We executed it like they would have done in the ‘30s and ‘40s."

Spreading Christmas cheer in July, Will Ferrell made some cheeky nods to his beloved Elf character Buddy while playing the Mattel CEO in the Barbie movie.

Among the discreet references to the 2003 comedy? He demands to be the one to press a button in the Mattel office elevator (calling back to the Elf scene where he presses every button in his dad's office building elevator, because the lights look "like a Christmas tree").

In Barbie, his suited character also starts a tickle fight—just like Buddy the Elf does with his dad Walter (James Caan) while being tucked into bed one night.

Going where no Barbie has gone before... The opening scene of Barbie pays homage to the 1968 Stanley Kubrick film 2001: A Space Odyssey, which shows a group of hominins discovering a futuristic monolith. In Barbie, a group of girls are shocked by a giant version of the original 1959 Barbie doll, wearing a black and white striped swimsuit.

Fans speculate that Gloria's daughter Sasha (Ariana Greenblatt) and her friends in the cafeteria were inspired by Barbie's rivals, the original Bratz dolls: Sasha, Chloe, Yasmin and Jade.

Casting director Allison Jones revealed Saturday Night Live star Bowen Yang, Schitt's Creek actor Dan Levy and Dear Evan Hansen actor Ben Platt almost played Kens in the movie but weren't able to make it work. She added, "They were, I'm not kidding, really bummed they couldn't do it."

According to the casting director, before Michael Cera came on board as Ken's buddy Allan, the part almost went to a certain Frozen actor.

"Dear, dear Jonathan Groff was like, 'I can't believe I'm typing this,'" Allison told Vanity Fair, "'but I can't do Allan.'"

America Ferrera's IRL husband Ryan Piers Williams plays none other than her character Gloria's husband. Ryan—whose past work includes producing, writing and acting in X/Y with America in 2014—is credited as "El Esposo de Gloria."

"It was a happy accident," John Cena told Today of his casting as a Mermaid Ken. He said he "kind of" pitched himself to join the film "in an accidental run-in with Margot Robbie."

As he recalled, he told the actress, "'I would do, pretty much, whatever you guys need 'cause I really enjoy the movie,' and they asked me if I wanted to be a merman."

The French version of Barbie's poster went viral after social media users pointed out the double entendre of the translation. The tagline, "She can do everything. He's just Ken," was translated to, "Elle peut tout faire. Lui, c'est juste Ken."

However, fans went wild after pointing out that "ken" has a slang meaning in French as "f--k" and would translate to, "He can only f--k." Bonjour, Ken!

The Barbie actresses had a cast sleepover at London hotel Claridge's to get close. "We all shared beds and wore our pajamas, and ordered room service," Margot revealed on The Kelly Clarkson Show, "and played games, and found out that America is exceptionally competitive."

America had her own tea to spill about the evening. "Nobody told me that it was a sexy Barbie sleepover," she quipped. "So everybody was in like really pretty silky nightgowns, and I was in like the most grandma floral twin set you can imagine."

As for the Kens? "Greta was very deliberate in what she wanted the Kens to do to bond," Simu Liu exclusively told E! News, "which was to gym together."

Though Nicola Coughlan only appeared for a few moments in the film, it was very important to her that she experience life in plastic.

"I auditioned for Barbie back in January '22 when I was on holiday with friends," she wrote on Instagram. "I'd packed one random hot pink dress I hadn't worn at all and when I had to make my audition tape I thought—this is fate, I have a dress in Barbie Pink!"

Admitting she's "obsessed" with Greta, the Bridgerton star said that "the prospect of working with her was something I couldn't even have imagined."

"When I found out she wanted to have me be part of @barbiethemovie, and then that I probably wouldn't be able to make it work because of my schedule I was firstly elated and quickly heartbroken," Nicola continued. "So when I was asked if I wanted to pop into Barbieland even briefly my answer was an immediate, and very emphatic yes."

The film concludes with Margot adopting a new life as a human named Barbara Handler, a reference to Barbie inventor Ruth Handler's real-life daughter. Barbie enters an office building and delivers her final line to a receptionist: "I'm here to see my gynecologist."

Why did Greta end on that note? "With this film, it was important for me that everything operated on at least two levels," she told USA Today. "I knew I wanted to end on a mic drop kind of joke, but I also find it very emotional. When I was a teenage girl, I remember growing up and being embarrassed about my body, and just feeling ashamed in a way that I couldn't even describe. It felt like everything had to be hidden."

The director hoped the way Margot delivered the line with a "big old smile on her face" and with "such happiness and joy" would help de-stigmatize conversations about women's health and "give girls that feeling of, 'Barbie does it, too'—that's both funny and emotional."

#820. Nottingham Forest’s historic goal drought at home is part of longstanding problem

Oliver Glasner’s side are yet to score at City Ground this season but troubles in front of goal precede his arrival

Nottingham Forest and Schalke are yet to score at home in 2026-27. The former are one of only five teams in the history of the English top flight to have failed to score in their first four home league matches. Three of the preceding four also drew a blank in game five, which will be deflating news for Oliver Glasner with Manchester City heading to the City Ground on Saturday looking for a win after consecutive league defeats. Forest’s expected goals total implies they should have scored but a flaw in their data shows a reason why.

They also failed to find the net in a Carabao Cup home game with Leeds, meaning they have amassed 70 shots in all competitions without giving the home fans a goal to celebrate. As extreme as this situation has become, Forest scored only two goals more than the lowest home scorers in the Premier League last season (Burnley), drawing a blank on nine occasions. This is a longstanding issue.

The dishonour of scoring the fewest home goals in Europe’s big five leagues in modern times belongs to Dijon, who bagged eight in 19 Ligue 1 games in 2020-21. Fulham went one goal better in the same season to claim the Premier League’s wooden spoon for home scoring. Both scored three across their first four games, showing the unlikely depths to which Forest’s attack has sunk at the City Ground.

With expected goals a frequent element of post-match analysis, it can be easy to overlook that shots are independent of each other. One is not more likely to be converted when those that preceded it were missed, even though the team’s xG total ticks upward. A side that produced one expected goal through 100 shots valued at 0.01 xG would be far from guaranteed to score.

This reality lies at the heart of Forest’s home woes. Their 62 league shots have been worth 3.58 expected goals. It may feel reasonable to assume they deserve three goals. But only two of the efforts were deemed by Opta to be big chances, only five more had a better than one-in-10 probability of being converted and more than two-thirds were valued at 0.06 xG or less. Only against Coventry did they muster at least one expected goal in total, needing 24 attempts to register 1.09 xG.

Forest’s chance quality is so poor because many of their efforts are struck from long range. They have taken 50.3% of their City Ground shots from outside the box, at least 6% more than any Premier League team did on their respective patch in any of the past five seasons.

Glasner’s side are having to do this because they are struggling to get the ball into the penalty area. Again, this is a problem that predates the Austrian’s appointment. Forest were below the league average of 36.6% for their home pass accuracy into the box in 2025-26 (33.3%) and have sunk lower this season (29.6%). Cross accuracy is not the most instructive metric because the most dangerous deliveries can evade teammates if they are not anticipating them. Nonetheless, Forest’s home data paints the same picture as with their passing; below league average (26.6%) for completion rate last season (21.7%) and worse again in 2026-27 (19.0%).

Having to shoot from distance has helped make them chronically unable to put shots on target. Forest have done this only nine times in the league at the City Ground, giving them a shot accuracy rate of 14.5%. It is unsurprising to see Schalke on 18.8% given they are equally goal-shy. The least accurate home side across the past 10 seasons of football in Europe’s big five leagues are the Parma class of 2025-26. Even they managed to put 23.7% of their shots on target when taking last place in a sample of 974 team season examples.

If Forest don’t score against City, their next opportunity will come against a Chelsea side that have recently tightened up. No English top flight side have failed to score in their first six home games but Forest setting this unwanted record looks distinctly possible.

#817. Bayern Munich's Kenya friendly highlights Africa's growing pull for global sport

Bayern Munich are to open Nairobi's new Raila Odinga International Stadium against Ajax as Kenya prepares for AFCON 2027. The match highlights Africa's growing sports ambitions — and questions over cost and legacy.

Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich are to travel to Nairobi, Kenya during the winter break to play a friendly that opens the newly finished Raila Odinga International Stadium in the capital city. The German side will face Ajax Amsterdam as the game acts as part of the country's preparations for the 2027 African Cup of Nations (AFCON), which will be held in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania next summer.

"Bayern has millions of fantastic fans in Africa with whom we feel a close connection – it's a continent with a huge passion for football," Rouven Kasper, Bayern board member for marketing and sales, said in a club statement.

"We will be making a further contribution to raising the profile of the Bundesliga and are very much looking forward to this special event."

The news is just the latest venture into global sports investing in Africa. Earlier this month, Formula 1 announced it was returning to the continent after Rwanda secured the rights for a deal from the early 2030s onwards. In September, World Athletics revealed Nairobi would host the World Championships in 2029. It will be the first time the event has been held in Africa.

Simon Chadwick, a business management and program director at the African School of Economics, believes that over the last two decades the professionalization and industrialization of sports has begun to emerge in Africa.

"Countries like Rwanda, Kenya, Morocco and obviously, South Africa, if we go back to the last decade of the previous century, have increasingly begun to deploy sport as a policy instrument," Chadwick told DW, adding Senegal and Egypt to the list.

"There are these image and reputational benefits which very often are bundled up as soft power. It's about attractiveness and appeal and engagement," said Chadwick.

"It's almost like a kind of professionalization, industrialization and politicization of sport that we're seeing elsewhere in the world has now arrived in Africa. We are seeing a much greater sense of kind of self-determination within Africa to do this," he added.

"This is not just about sport. It is also about diplomacy and bilateral trade, but also about the broader economic and industrial context within which sport sits."

For Kenya specifically, the building of the stadium is in line with the housing and sports infrastructural development that has been so heavily promoted under President William Ruto. Hosting this game is a symbol of the development currently happening in Nairobi.

"The bigger picture is that Nairobi now is positioning itself as a as an alternative sports venue," Richard Wanjohi, Editorial and Research Lead at the African Sports and Creative Institute (ASCI), told DW.

"I think we have seen what Kigali has done over the last number of years. For us to then come back into this conversation as a major city that can host such an event, it's huge. A few weeks later, we'll have the rugby sevens series again and then ultimately, the Africa Cup of Nations in July."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chadwick believes that unlike Rwanda, Kenya's relative stability and pre-existing tourist industry allows for a more natural development of sports investment.

"This is not Kenya trying to build a tourism industry through an engagement in sport. I think it's an extension of what Kenya has been doing for a number of years through sport."

Combined with being a multi-sport country - athletics, rugby, football, volleyball – Wanjohi believes Kenya is ready to make the most of that performance on the field or track.

"It's about time that we also host the world and show them that we can do this from a hosting perspective, but also from developing infrastructure that is ready to host such sports events," Wanjohi said.

"It's beyond just saying that we have the talent that is already in the sport, but it's saying that we have the infrastructure, we have the skills, we have the capability to host this as any other African, if not global nation."

However, Ruto's government has been criticized over taxation, unemployment and its handling of dissent. Given that this stadium cost approximately €375 million ($418 million), it is perhaps no surprise that questions are being asked about the decision to invest in major sports infrastructure.

"People are asking, we are a struggling economy. There are a lot of other issues that could be addressed, like the education sector, health and all that. How did we get that money and be able to make that provision? Also interestingly, is that there's an appearance fee that is going to be paid to both Bayern and Ajax," said Wanjohi, who added there was also some frustration that the opening game was not given to local teams or even the national side.

Ultimately, the timing of this also matters. While many sports fans in the country are excited, others are critical.

"The government knows that this is almost like a campaign tool. We have an election coming up in August next year so the government or the president of the day obviously wants to use as much leverage of such an event to milk it for all it's worth," Wanjohi added.

"So the two different schools of thought are: It's a good thing to have, but at what cost are we doing it at and is it in the public interest as well?"

The proof will be in what the legacy of events like Bayern Munich's friendly in Nairobi brings Kenyan football. The feeling in late 2026 though, is largely optimistic.

"I guess the acid test is that many African nations carry with them the baggage from the past that this is just trophy asset investment that is ultimately going to create white, white elephant infrastructure," Chadwick said.

"But having spoken to people in Kenyan sport, in the industry itself, it seems to me that there is a genuine appetite for sports to become a genuine and legitimate driver of economic activity."

Janek Speight contributed reporting for this article.

#816. The palaeo cave art that hid in plain sight for 26,000 years

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chris Simms is a science writer based in Somerset, UK.

Inscriptions at the Cova de la Font Major cave system in Catalonia in northeastern Spain prompts rethink of prehistoric population and cultural trends. Credit: Vergès Bosch, J. M., Salas-Altès, M./Antiquity

Inscriptions at the Cova de la Font Major cave system in Catalonia in northeastern Spain prompts rethink of prehistoric population and cultural trends. Credit: Vergès Bosch, J. M., Salas-Altès, M./Antiquity

Archaeologists have described hundreds of rock-art engravings dating back around 26,000 years in a cave frequently visited by tourists in Catalonia — a region of northeastern Spain that was thought to be almost devoid of palaeolithic art1. The findings were published in the journal Antiquity on 5 November.

Josep Maria Vergès Bosch, an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) in Tarragona, Spain, spotted some prehistoric engravings among more-modern graffiti in the Cova de la Font Major during a planned excavation in 2019.

Vergès and archaeologist Míriam Salas-Altès at IPHES-CERCA studied 280 Palaeolithic art motifs, including 55 animal depictions, from the cave. “The sheer quantity of art discovered at the Cova de la Font Major is exceptional,” says Salas-Altès.

The cave system — made up of more than 3.5 kilometres of underground passageways that have been occupied numerous times during human history — has been open to the public for some seven decades and became a museum in the 1990s.

The drawings were easy to miss. “When you shine a light straight on the engravings, they are really difficult to see, you have to play with light from different directions to see the depressions,” says Salas-Altès.

Researcher Míriam Salas-Altès documents engravings in a tunnel of the cave system. Credit: Josep Maria Vergès/IPHES-CERCA

The etchings include images of animals such as a horse, a bear and an aurochs (the ancestor of domestic cattle), as well as myriad swirling lines. A handful of the engravings reveal how the artists used “natural lines or fissures in the walls”, says Salas-Altès. For example, “one is used to represent the ground under a horse”.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03585-z

Vergès Bosch, J. M. & Salas-Altès, M. Antiquity https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2026.10447 (2027).
