#718. Preprint platform offers to pay researchers to review papers, but questions remain

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Paying researchers to review papers is seen as a potential solution to clearing the peer-reviewing backlog.Credit: UpPiJ/iStock via Getty

A preprint platform is paying researchers for reviewing preprints uploaded by other scientists, reigniting debates about whether peer reviewers should be paid.

XSci, which launched in September, will reward a reviewer with US$200 if they send their feedback within five days of accepting the task and $100 if they do so between five and ten days. The fee is covered by other researchers, who pay XSci to have their preprints reviewed by scholars. The preprint website, which does not publish a journal, charges each author $399 for a round of review or $249 if they make their review report public.

The system enables authors to receive comments quickly while compensating reviewers for their time and effort, says Shumiao Ouyang, the founder of XSci, the start-up firm incorporated in Delaware that runs the platform. The company has received around $500,000 from private investors and is trying to raise more funds, Ouyang says.

A publishing platform that places code front and centre

A publishing platform that places code front and centre

“What authors get is an answer, usually within about five to ten days, to the question they care about most: does this paper have a real chance at the journals I am aiming at? Today, that answer can take months, and in some fields, years,” says Ouyang, who is an economist at the University of Oxford, UK. XSci also charges authors up to $19 to have their preprints reviewed by a range of artificial-intelligence programs, although access to some AI tools is free.

Several researchers interviewed by Nature say that XSci’s business model is interesting, but that its future will depend mostly on whether it can attract authors to use its human-reviewing service.

“Will authors be willing to pay such a fee? Where does the money come from?” asks developmental biologist and toxicologist Daniel Gorelick at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, Texas, who has served as editor-in-chief of Biology Open since July 2023.

But Gorelick also says that cash payments are “a powerful incentive”. Biology Open, an open-access journal published by The Company of Biologists, has been paying reviewers £220 (or $280) per manuscript since 2024 through a programme called Fast and Fair. The payment is issued to the reviewer if they send in their work on time and if its quality meets the editors’ expectations.

Ouyang expects XSci’s core authors to be doctoral and postdoctoral students, as well as early-career researchers “who often cannot wait for a year or more for a journal’s decision”.

Peer reviewers are conventionally expected to review manuscripts as a service to the scientific community, rather than for a fee. By paying them at the preprint stage, Ouyang says, XSci intends to tackle challenges that dog the academic publishing industry today: how to convince scholars to review the work of others and to do it quickly.

Several studies1–3 have shown that journal editors are finding it increasingly difficult to source reviewers for various reasons, including a rising number of submissions and academics’ growing workloads. These and other issues often lead to a long review time, which can range from a few weeks to several months.

XSci states on its website that academics can register their interest to be paid reviewers. But in reality, says Ouyang, a scholar must be invited by the website to review a manuscript. The website nevertheless has a ‘register interest’ field for practical reasons because, he explains, “it tells us how many willing researchers there are in each field.”

Shumiao Ouyang is an economist at the University of Oxford, UK, and founder of XSci.Credit: Yizhen Zhang

Ouyang says that XSci has developed an AI program to help find suitable reviewers quickly. Once an author uploads their manuscript to XSci and chooses the human-reviewing option, the AI tool will compile a ranking of potential reviewers by screening candidates from three sources: the scientists who wrote the papers that the manuscript cites, those scholars’ regular collaborators and researchers who have published papers on similar topics in the author’s target journals. The AI program will rank, then e-mail, potential reviewers one by one. Each potential reviewer has 12 hours to accept the job, says Ouyang.

If the reviewer thinks that the manuscript could be published in the author’s target journals after reasonable changes, the preprint will be given a badge on the website, demonstrating that it has been reviewed and is endorsed by the reviewer.

In time, XSci hopes to form partnerships with journal publishers that would allow the journals’ editors to use XSci’s review reports as part of their assessments. This would happen only if the authors and reviewers both agree to the reports being shared, Ouyang says. The idea is that editors can decide what to do with XSci’s reviews: whether to use them to replace one round of their own reviews or as external references, he adds. In follow-up questions from Nature, however, Ouyang stressed that the badge would merely “become useful information for an editor”.

“Whether a journal gives them any weight is the entirely the journal’s decision,” he added.

In 2025, Fast and Fair helped to slash the time that Biology Open editors spent making the first decision about a manuscript from an average of 37.7 working days under the free-reviewing route to an average of 5.5 working days, according to a preprint co-authored by Gorelick4. The programme also led to review invitations having a higher acceptance rate and a higher completion rate of accepted tasks, the study found.

But a separate study found that paying reviewers did not achieve substantial improvements. Editors at Critical Care Medicine, a journal published by Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, carried out a six-month experiment in which they sent reviewers invitations with or without monetary incentives in alternating two-week blocks5. They found that 50% of review invitations with a $250 cash reward resulted in a peer-review report in 14 days, compared with 42% of invitations without the fee. Paid reviewers also delivered their work just one day quicker on average than did non-paid reviewers.

“It didn’t move the needle too much,” says David Maslove, one of the editors who co-authored in the study and a clinician-scientist at Queen’s University in Kingston, Canada.

‘Getting paid to review is justice’: journal pays peer reviewers in cryptocurrency

‘Getting paid to review is justice’: journal pays peer reviewers in cryptocurrency

A paying system comes with challenges, researchers warn. There need to be stringent quality controls, as well as policies in place to ensure that reviewers don’t game the system and publishers don’t take advantage of reviewers, Gorelick says. “You can’t just pay reviewers and walk away,” he notes.

“XSci currently does not check the quality of the reviews done by the reviewers before they are released to the authors,” says Jeffery Poon, publishing and editorial lead of XSci. If the authors are not satisfied with what they receive, they can initiate an appeal through XSci, Poon notes. XSci plans to provide tools to reviewers to help them check their own work, but the team is still working out how that could be implemented in reality, he adds.

How "Forrest Gump", pizza, and a massive supporting cast of furballs came together to make one of "Star Trek"'s finest hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history, but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment.

Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney).

But it was "DS9"'s "Trials and Tribble-ations" that turned out to be the more memorable voyage to "Trek" past, as Captain Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) — with the help of some then-state-of-the-art digital trickery — came face-to-face with a young Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner).

While "Flashback" aired within days of "Trek"'s September 8 birthday, fans had to wait a little longer for "DS9"'s contribution to the celebrations. Showrunner Ira Steven Behr was keen to avoid disrupting the space station-set drama's story arc for a comedic diversion, meaning that "Trials and Tribble-ations" didn't debut until November 4, 1996.

In the wake of "Flashback" — not to mention Spock and Scotty's comebacks in "The Next Generation" stories "Unification" and "Relics" — the "DS9" writers' room had already decided they needed to take a very different approach.

Early on, "Battlestar Galactica" creator Ronald D. Moore pitched a follow-up to Original Series episode "A Piece of the Action" (aka the one where the residents of Iotia brought 1920s gangsters to life). In an extremely meta concept that predated "Galaxy Quest" by three years, the story would have taken the Enterprise crew to a planet of Kirk and Spock impersonators.

"For the thirtieth anniversary, you go back, and you're basically going back to the planet of 'Star Trek' fans," Moore recalled in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A. Altman and Edward Gross. "They have conventions; they know all the adventures. It's a phenomenon, and you could comment on 'Star Trek' as a whole. I thought it would be interesting. But [fellow writer] René Echevarria thought it was a dangerous show to do, that we would be talking down to the fans on some level, and perhaps it wasn't the best way to go."

Instead, Echevarria suggested telling a story in the vein of Woody Allen's "Zelig" or "Forrest Gump" (then a zeitgeisty, multi-Oscar-winning box-office smash) and integrating the "Deep Space Nine" crew with the events of an Original Series episode.

"I thought, 'What bigger treat could there be than to go back into the past and board the original Enterprise and have a mission there?'" Echevarria said in a 1996 making-of documentary. "And Ron immediately said, 'It's gotta be "The Trouble with Tribbles!"'"

"The Trouble with Tribbles", a 1967 episode from "Star Trek"'s second season, is one of the most famous in the franchise's history. As well as featuring some minor scuffles with Klingons, it sees the Enterprise and Deep Space Station K-7 infested with the eponymous tribbles — cute, cuddly furballs of calm that reproduce at a dangerously exponential rate.

In "Trials and Tribble-ations", a timey-wimey incident involving the Bajoran Orb of Time transports the USS Defiant (one of the best "Star Trek" spaceships) back to the era of Kirk and Spock's famous five-year mission.

As Sisko recounts the adventure to a pair of agents from Starfleet's Department of Temporal Investigations (named Dulmur and Lucsly in homage to "The X-Files"), we learn how he, Dax (Terry Farrell), O'Brien (Colm Meaney), and Bashir (Alexander Siddig) spent a day playing Original Series cosplay on Kirk's Enterprise. It's "Star Trek"'s answer to "Back to the Future: Part II", as the crew interacts with established events while taking pains not to mess with history.

Although most of the guest stars from "The Trouble with Tribbles" had passed away over the intervening decades, one actor who'd played a pivotal role was still around. By the time he turned up in "Star Trek", 20-something stand-up comedian Charlie Brill had already brushed shoulders with pop-culture legend, having shared the bill with the Beatles when they made their famous appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" in February 1964.

Three years later he'd swapped Lennon and McCartney for Kirk and Spock, playing a Klingon spy masquerading as human Arne Darvin, whose cover is ultimately blown by the famously Klingon-phobic tribbles. In the newer episode, the older Darvin travels back in time to assassinate Kirk, plotting his revenge with a bomb implanted in an unfortunate tribble. Thwarting the evil scheme — and preserving the timeline — forms the basis of Sisko's mission.

Brill's return was seemingly written in the stars. When planning the episode, Behr and the other writers met for lunch at Mulberry Street Pizza in Beverly Hills and noted that the actor was alive and still working in the business. Then, just as they were talking about him, they happened to spot Brill across the very same restaurant.

"What were the chances that we would be talking about this old TV episode from 30 years ago, and the guy who we were talking about to bring back on the show would be standing there ordering a slice of pizza?" Behr recalled at the Trek Talks telethon (via TrekMovie).

But however strong its story, "Trials and Tribble-ations" was always going to live and die by its recreation of ' 60s-era "Trek". The production team subsequently pulled out all the stops, with Behr suggesting at the time that it may have been the most expensive hour of TV ever made.

The actors were kitted out in era-appropriate primary-colored outfits and given '60s hairdos. The make-up team also recreated the appearance of the Original Series' Klingons, whose very different look — "We do not discuss it with outsiders," says Worf — would later be explained away in a "Star Trek: Enterprise" two-parter.

The late Walter Koenig (who'd featured as Chekov in "The Trouble with Tribbles") showed the younger officers how to flip open a communicator, and the stunt team choreographed fights to look like the cheesy, Western-inspired brawls of a bygone era.

Behind the scenes, production designer Michael Okuda and his team used a mixture of original plans and scans of the episodes to painstakingly recreate the sets, while the visual effects team constructed an exact half-scale replica of the original 11-foot Enterprise shooting model housed in the Smithsonian.

The biggest magic trick, however, was dependent on CG technology — then very much in its infancy — making everyone believe that Sisko and co were walking the same corridors as Kirk. VFX supervisor Gary Hutzel had provided proof-of-concept early in the process:

"He showed us a clip from the old show," said Behr. "We looked at it and said, 'Okay, that looks good, but what does that have to do with us?' And he said, 'Well, you see that guy coming in through the door? That's not from the 1967 episode. That's one of our people!'"

Shooting in front of blue- and green-screens, the actors' performances were meticulously matched to the Original Series episode. Early on, Moore had identified two sequences from "The Trouble with Tribbles" that would be perfect for selling the concept: Kirk dressing down a line-up of officers after a bar room brawl and Tribbles raining down on Kirk from a storage container.

O'Brien and Bashir were digitally pasted over the original actors in the former, while the latter was explained away by Sisko and Dax's madcap dash to find the elusive explosive tribble. In most other shots, the DS9ers became background observers in existing scenes.

But there were still debates to be had over whether the two captains should meet. "It led to one of the most vociferous arguments we've had," said Behr, a passionate advocate for the "yes" camp. "We were so deadlocked, and there was so much emotion in the air, we actually turned to the writer intern and said, ‘What do you think?’ End of stalemate. Of course, being an intern and being a smart guy, he sided with his executive producer. And life went on." (The scene in which Sisko hands Kirk a duty roster for approval was actually lifted from another Original Series episode, "Mirror, Mirror", with Brooks replacing Barbara Luna (Lt. Marlena Moreau) on the bridge.)

It was all worth the effort. "Trials and Tribble-ations" was the most-watched episode of "DS9"'s fifth season, bagged nominations for three Emmys and a Hugo, and is now widely regarded as one of the best "Trek" episodes of all time.

David Gerrold, who wrote "The Trouble with Tribbles" and appeared as an extra in "Trials and Tribble-ations", described it as "possibly the best episode of 'Star Trek' after the Original Series," and various members of the writers' room have described it as a highlight of their time on the final frontier.

"From the writers to the director to the lighting, costumes, the set, sound effects, visual effects — everybody really put in so much time on that episode to really recreate the original Enterprise in any way they possibly could," said Moore. "Everybody was staring at film clips, doing research into [prop/costume] materials. It was a mania, and everybody just threw themselves into it. They wanted to make it great. And it shows."

'The Trouble with Tribbles' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' are available to stream on Paramount+ in both the US and UK.

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

The MCU’s Multiverse Saga is nearly over, but there are plenty more Marvel movies and shows on the horizon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Marvel fatigue? Think again, especially after Spider-Man: Brand New Day made over $2.5 billion worldwide and Avengers: Doomsday is looking hot, hot, hot!

But even after the uneven Multiverse Saga ends (hopefully on a high note), Marvel Studios won’t be stopping. So, we've put together a list of all the upcoming MCU movies and shows confirmed so far.

While the MCU isn't stopping, Marvel has slowed its roll, with the powers that be returning to the “quality over quantity” approach that defined Marvel Studios’ Infinity Saga output. This means no more than three movies per year and, perhaps more importantly, severely cutting down on TV productions, with a focus on multi-season shows rather than limited series that should’ve been a movie.

It’s a time of change for both Disney and Marvel, but it seems everyone agrees the big screen reigns supreme, so expect a thinner streaming output and more relevant movies starring characters you actually know.

More will be revealed in due time, but for now, here’s what lies at the Multiverse Saga’s end and beyond...

Release date: December 18, 2026 | Director: Anthony & Joe Russo | Cast: Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Pedro Pascal, Robert Downey Jr.

Earth’s Mightiest Heroes (from different Earths, actually) are assembling again in December 2026.

Avengers: Doomsday's cast looks ridiculously stacked, and it’ll finally realize the dream of bringing together the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, and the X-Men (Fox’s original ones, that is) on the big screen. It’s a lot to absorb, and we don’t really know what's going on, but the trailers released so far are promising.

Anthony & Joe Russo (Captain America: The Winter Soldier & Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War & Endgame) are returning to direct, so that’s a good reason to be hyped even if the duo’s post-Marvel career hasn’t been the most exciting. Stephen McFeely (one of their two go-to scribes) is also back, and Michael Waldron (Loki) is helping out as well. It’s an all-star team for the most ambitious MCU project to date, at least until it all culminates in...

Release window: March 2027 | Showrunner: Dario Scardapane | Cast: Charlie Cox, Mike Colter, Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter

Daredevil: Born Again’s debut season was far from perfect, but most viewers agreed that Season 2 was a marked improvement.

Hopefully, that energy will continue in the third and final outing, as the Defenders reunite, with Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter, and Mike Colter all returning from their Netflix shows. Another shocker is the (unofficially) confirmed return of Elodie Yung’s Elektra.

We suspect some of these characters will be transferred to movies post-Secret Wars. In any case, Born Again’s final season should be packed, especially if Marvel Television is sticking to eight or nine episodes.

Release date: December 17, 2027 | Director: Anthony & Joe Russo | Cast: Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Pedro Pascal, Robert Downey Jr.

Practically nothing about the follow-up to Avengers: Doomsday has been revealed yet (though we assume the MCU’s main players will be part of the ensemble), but we know it fully starts shooting in late 2026 and is eyeing a Christmas 2027 arrival. The plan is to leave a year-long wait between the two event movies, leaving fans hanging like back in the MCU’s glory days.

The title comes from Jonathan Hickman’s Secret Wars (2015), which is probably the main source of inspiration for the upcoming big-screen event. Incursions (realities bleeding into each other) have already been set up during the Multiverse Saga, and we know Doomsday directly deals with the multiverse’s breaking point, so it’s easy to see where the larger picture is going.

No spoilers here, but prepare for a very different kind of Avengers flick if Battleworld is indeed the main setting.

Release date: May 5, 2028 | Director: Jake Schreier | Cast: Kit Connor, Sadie Sink, Adam Driver, Christopher Abbott

Whatever happens in Secret Wars (we’ve heard Marvel Studios intends to soft-reboot), Phase Seven of the MCU will kick off with a long-awaited, fresh take on the X-Men — now part of the larger Marvel universe housing all characters. Thunderbolts* director Jake Schreier will be directing, with the same writing team from that movie joining him for another Marvel adventure.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day already did some heavy lifting when it came to setting up one of its leads (Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey), but it’s unclear how the whole group will be assembled.

We know for sure Cyclops (Kit Connor), Rogue (Inde Navarrette), Emma Frost (Samara Weaving), Storm (Maya Boyd), Angel (Asa Germann), Charles Xavier (Christopher Abbott), and Mr. Sinister (Adam Driver) are confirmed to appear, but the cast should grow in the coming months.

Release date: July 28, 2028 | Director: Shawn Levy | Cast: Ryan Gosling (more to be confirmed)

Phase Seven’s second movie will be an unexpected one, but the fan reaction to its reveal was glowing: Ghost Rider, starring Ryan Gosling, with Deadpool & Wolverine’s Shawn Levy directing.

The duo worked together on Star Wars: Starfighter, and it seems it went so well that Disney and Marvel are happy with them reviving the Spirit of Vengeance as the MCU expands its dark borders.

It’s too early to even know which Ghost Rider that Gosling will be playing (Johnny Blaze or Danny Ketch) or where the plot is going, but considering Levy’s past movies, we’re expecting an adventurous tone that blends well with Ghost Rider’s very striking, hellish visuals and darker themes.

Of course, this project is an invitation to add more magical beings to the MCU and explore the Strange-adjacent side of it. Maybe it’s our first step towards a Midnight Sons event movie? We can only hope.

Release date: December 15, 2028 | Director: Ryan Coogler | Cast: David Jonsson, Denzel Washington, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke

Ryan Coogler has taken a break from Marvel to make the excellent Sinners and help create a new iteration of The X-Files, but he’s confirmed to be coming back to wrap up his epic Black Panther trilogy. A while back, he confirmed he’d convinced Denzel Washington to join the MCU, and it sounds like those plans haven’t changed.

We also have a new T’Challa: David Jonsson (Alien: Romulus), who’s meant to play the son of the original T’Challa (Chadwick Boseman). If the years don’t make sense considering he was a kid in Wakanda Forever, wait until Secret Wars’ “soft reboot” for the answers.

What we know for sure is that series veterans Letitia Wright and Winston Duke are expected to stick around, but no plot details are available yet.

Release window: 2028 | Showrunner: Unconfirmed | Cast: Unconfirmed

Revealed at NYCC 2026, Zodiac is set to be Marvel Television’s next ongoing series after Daredevil: Born Again is over. Little is known about the premise at this point, though TV boss Brad Winderbaum has confirmed it’s a “globetrotting, international espionage show about secrets and lies and betrayals” with a packed cast of characters.

Word is the show is, more specifically, a British spy thriller with three leads, two male and one female. It’s expected to shoot in London during spring 2027, and chances are we’ll know much more about it well before that.

Of course, longtime Marvel TV fans are hoping for an Agents of SHIELD revival of sorts (its canonicity was never entirely clear), but it seems this show isn’t exactly that, though Clark Gregg (Agent Coulson) might be involved.

We’ve learned to never say never when it comes to Marvel comebacks, so stay tuned for more news.

Release windows: October 2027 / October 2028 / October 2029 | Showrunner: Bryan Andrews | Cast: Unconfirmed

Following a four-episode season in 2025, the animated series Marvel Zombies will be returning for three consecutive years (starting in 2027) just in time for Halloween.

The twist is that we’re now looking at three two-part specials: The Winter Soldier, The Fist of Khonshu, and The Last Guardian. It’s a huge departure from the previous plans with the Zombies and What If...? series, but it's one that could pay off.

Nothing is known about these small-scale projects at this point, but we know Marvel Zombies was a large enough hit on Disney+ to warrant more, and we’re okay with being surprised when it comes to format.

One has to assume these specials could work as one-shot comic books, but it’ll be interesting to see whether Marvel Television can tell cohesive and compelling stories with even shorter story arcs.

"The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

President Trump issued a declaration yesterday (Nov. 3), proclaiming space open to all humanity for exploration, and the right of American citizens to develop and settle the solar system according to United States laws.

"The American Declaration of Freedom in Space," describes space as the "province of all humans" and asserts that the United States will lead humanity's expansion into the cosmos. The proclamation reiterates the administration's goals with NASA's Artemis program to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 and eventually sending astronauts to Mars, but introduces no new funding, programs or policy directives.

"Our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers — forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty," the document says.

Trump invoked America's "frontier spirit," highlighting Apollo 11 astronauts as the first people in history to walk on the moon's surface and robotic rovers exploring Mars as examples of U.S. leadership, and emphasized the country's flourishing commercial space sector helping ensure "American space superiority for all eternity."

"The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity," the declaration says, and pledges that America will carry the values of faith, freedom and individual liberty into an interplanetary civilization.

The proclamation also highlights the success of NASA's Artemis II mission in April, which carried four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon and set a record for the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth. The follow-up to that mission, Artemis III, is scheduled to launch next summer (2027), and will test rendezvous and docking operations between NASA's Orion spacecraft and the program's two commercial lunar landers in low Earth orbit.

Artemis IV will be the program's first lunar landing mission, and is targeted for 2028. A December 2025 executive order from the President reaffirmed the goal of meeting that timeline, as well as the deployment of the initial elements for a permanent lunar outpost by 2030.

Trump's declaration yesterday does not establish new NASA programs, allocate additional funding or issue instructions to federal agencies. Its sweeping language, though, does echo some of the principles in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which guarantees freedom of exploration while prohibiting national sovereignty claims on other planets.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#712. Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union

Kazakhstan is struggling to deal with the legacy of the Soviet dictatorship. Some 85 years ago, Stalin deported hundreds of thousands of people: Some 400,000 ethnic Germans living in the USSR were sent to Kazakhstan.

She wants to keep history alive. Yunna Kinereish, 22, is studying public relations in Kazakhstan's modern capital, Astana. She describes herself as a Kazakh German.

"I am German by ethnicity. But I also feel that I'm Kazakh, because I keep the traditions with my family, and I have this mentality," she told DW.

Kinereish, who belongs to the Wiedergeburt (Revival) Association of Germans in Kazakhstan, is one of 223,000 Kazakh Germans living in the Central Asian republic of Kazakhstan today.

Kinereish recently acted in a play at the association's youth theater that told the fate of her Russian German forebears.

From the 18th century onward, Germans were incentivized to leave Germany and settle in the Russian empire, including in Ukraine's Black Sea region.

But after the armies of Hitler's Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, Soviet dictator Josef Stalin started deporting hundreds of thousands of Germans living in Russia and Ukraine to Siberia and Kazakhstan.

Innocent people who had nothing to do with Nazi Germany's invasion and atrocities were collectively held responsible by the Soviet power and denounced as spies and collaborators.

There were more than a million deportees, of whom at least 200,000 died as a result of expulsion, hunger, and forced labor.

"My family is part of this history, these terrible times. They were driven out of the Ukrainian village Kleinwärter, a settlement of ethnic Germans in Ukraine."

Yunna Kinereish says she was very moved by the personal stories she and her friends had brought to the stage at the House of Friendship, where the association has its office. "It's not easy for me, because it all touches my heart very deeply. I actually feel like crying. But when I'm on stage ..., I have to be strong."

The modern-looking House of Friendship in the capital Astana is the center for German culture in the city. Financed primarily by the German government, it offers language courses, engages in social work and fosters a culture of remembrance, focusing on the themes of deportation and repression under the Soviet regime.

Yunna Kinereish doesn't only present the history of her people on stage: She is also documenting it on film. In 2025, she made a film about German women incarcerated in ALZhIR (Akmolinsk Camp for Wives of Traitors to the Motherland), among the most infamous in the Soviet Gulag system.

During Stalin's brutal campaign of political repression and state-sponsored terror in the 1930s, a period known as the Great Terror, the Soviet Union established its biggest camp system in Kazakhstan. 18,000 women passed through the ALZhIR camp alone. These women were imprisoned there only because their husbands had been convicted of being traitors or enemies of the people. Among them were 167 ethnic German women, whose stories are told in the film.

The memorial for the ALZhIR women's camp is located just outside the gates of Astana, which only became the capital in 1997.

Astana's roads are permanently clogged with traffic. There are almost no pedestrians, and no cyclists at all. The city is growing, with new buildings shooting up all along the outskirts of the city. Beyond them is the barren steppe; the village of Akmol is about an hour's drive away.

Before entering the actual ALZhIR museum, the visitor passes through the Arch of Grief, a huge steel construction that commemorates the suffering and forced labor the women endured. The museum itself contains personal items that belonged to the female prisoners, models of their primitive quarters, original documents and photographs.

One of the photos is of Gertrud Platais, a woman with German roots who spent years incarcerated in ALZhIR. Platais was a print worker from Lower Silesia, part of modern-day Poland. She married Karl Eduard Platais and became a Soviet citizen. In 1938, during the Great Terror, her husband was arrested. Gertrud was convicted, too as a "relative of a traitor to the homeland."

She was transferred to ALZhIR, in a region where temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer and minus 40 degreees Celsius in winter. Here, she was forced to work as an embroiderer until 1946. After this, she was banished for life to the huge Karaganda Corrective Labor Camp, known as Karlag. Gertrud Platais wasn't rehabilitated until 1956. Hers is just one story documenting the terror of the Soviet system on Kazakh soil.

Karlag was by far the biggest camp system, and its complex covered an area about 22 times the size of New York City. Karlag was not just a prison camp, but a huge economic and agricultural complex. Almost one million people passed through it between 1931 and 1959.

Around 10,000 prisoners are believed to have died here between 1940 and 1950 alone: of starvation, cold, sickness, and the effects of forced labor.

The museum sits in the middle of the Kazakh steppe, near the city of Karaganda, about 250 kilometers south of Astana. It is located in the building that used to house the camp system administration. Visiting German historians and specialists are slightly puzzled: People were not tortured or tormented in this building, it was simply where the administration was done.

Here, interrogation and torture cells have been reconstructed, and everything is underscored by melodramatic music pouring from ubiquitous loudspeakers. It comes across as staged rather than authentic. As at the ALZhIR memorial, the Karlag museum has few visitors. Even well-educated young Kazakhs probably don't know about it."

Many people in Kazakhstan, and certain areas of politics, have almost no interest in coming to terms with the country's often brutal history," says Katherine M. Erdman. An American anthropologist and archaeologist at the Nazarbayev University in Astana, she has been researching the Gulag system for about a decade now.

"We wanted to find out where exactly the camps were, and how they can still be recognized today." Erdman and her students relied on modern technology such as drone flights, but conducting interviews and research on the ground was also a part of it.

"In many regions, the landscape has been shaped by forced labor," Erdman says. Factories were often constructed alongside the primitive living quarters. Houses were built using bricks made by forced laborers.

The researchers share their findings directly with neighbors and with local administrations. "Often we're just met with apathy, or flat-out rejection," says Erdman. At a time of economic and social advancement, many don't want to be reminded of the inglorious aspects of the past.

Erdman says there is a desire to demonstrate to the international community that the country is dealing with the dark side of its history, but that she often experiences lack of interest and even rejection. The academic has been conducting research in Kazakhstan for a decade, but there is no state funding for a further lectureship.

The Kazakh German Yunna Kinereish is one of the young people in Kazakhstan who want to ensure that the past is not forgotten. "My ancestors survived the Gulag system in Kazakhstan," she tells DW. "So it's important to me that we don't forget our roots, and that what our forefathers experienced and suffered is passed on."

This article, originally published in German, was written in the context of a study trip organized by the Federal Foundation for the Study of the Communist Dictatorship in Germany. Since 1998, the foundation, funded by the German taxpayer, has dedicated itself to studying and reappraising the former communist dictatorships in Germany, the GDR, and other countries.

#710. On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force

Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan.

For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket. The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff.

Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor.

The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms. After failing to launch this batch of cubesats, the Super Strypi program never recovered from its failure, and the Air Force never tried launching another one.

The Super Strypi rocket was a 21st century take on a 1960s rocket. It was designed to be a modern version of the three-stage Strypi sounding rocket used for for reentry vehicle and anti-missile target tests. Its three stages, powered by Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors, was designed to reach orbit, rather than suborbital trajectories common to most sounding rockets.

The U.S. Air Force hoped Super Strypi would be a new tool for quick-response launches based on national security needs. Altogether, it was designed to launch small payloads of up to 300 kilograms into space for a mere $15 million per mission.

The rocket's primary payload was the ORS-4 satellite, short for Operationally Responsive Space 4, which was built for the Air Force by engineers at the University of Hawaii (who nicknamed it HiakaSat). It was designed to capture Earth imagery and monitor the environment over the course of a year.

The 12 other payloads on Super Strypi included eight cubesats for NASA's Edison Demonstration of Smallsat Networks mission, and as well as four others for universities that had been added as secondary payloads.

Since the Super Strypi failure, neither the Air Force or Space Force has opted to use the rocket for a new mission. The Space Force has turned instead to commercial companies for fast-turnaround launch support.

In June of this year, the U.S. Space Force teamed up with Rocket Lab to launch the Victus Haze mission with just 17 hours of notice, a new record to demonstrate short-turnaround launch response.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#709. Albert Brooks Predicted Ozempic. Now He’s Predicting President Ossoff

In his 2011 novel 'Twenty Thirty,' he imagined a blockbuster weight-loss drug, a generational war — and a Jewish president. "God damn it," he recently told a friend. "My entire book is going to come true.”

By the fifth sentence of Twenty Thirty, Albert Brooks already looks like a modern-day Nostradamus. At an 80th birthday party in the 2011 novel, everyone looks suspiciously good, due in part to “a new weight-loss drug” that “works almost 100 percent of the time, in everyone.”

Then come the computer watches, the self-driving vehicles and a generation of young people furious at their elders for living so long and consuming so much of the country’s wealth.

But the prediction that gave the director of Lost in America chills was the one about a Jewish president. Related Stories Midterms 2026 How Jon Ossoff Won Re-Election and Became the Midterms' Main Character in the Process General News Albert Brooks Reacts to Rob Reiner's Murder: "I'm Still in That Not Believing It Stage"

In the novel, a candidate named Matthew Bernstein, the son of a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother, wins the 2028 election and becomes America’s first Jewish president. Brooks, 79, was watching Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff’s final campaign speech when he thought of Bernstein. Ossoff also has a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother. Brooks called a close friend.

“God damn it,” he remembers saying. “My entire book is going to come true.”

I’d read and loved Twenty Thirty, and Ossoff made me think of Bernstein, too. So I called Brooks to ask how much of the future he imagined in 2011 he thinks we’re already living in.

Albert, what made you give your president a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother?

When one parent is one religion and one parent is another, it sort of puts you in a third place. You come from two ends of a spectrum, and as a result, you experience more in life. And that’s what Ossoff is. In my opinion, he produces exactly the feeling as when Obama emerged. This guy talks to an audience as good as anyone I’ve ever heard.

The thing that gets him elected in the book is that his opponent is heard on a hot mic saying something antisemitic.

Right. So the only difference is that today that might be a plus.

Well, let me ask you that. There’s so much antisemitism now. How do you think that could affect someone like Jon Ossoff?

I’ve watched him speak many, many times now and it doesn’t come up. It doesn’t even go there. He is so captivating, in the way he explains to an audience why they’re feeling the way they do.

He doesn’t talk to people coming from a religious place. He talks to people about their pocketbook and about their Medicare and about stuff that they’re really concerned about.

Again, it was like when Obama emerged. The early questions were, “Well, could this happen? An African American?” But it never came up with Obama because he was so captivating and people were just interested in how, maybe, he was going to fix their lives.

Of course with Obama, race did come up, but he overcame that.

Obama came on the scene and talked to you differently than anyone else, and that’s why you listened. And he was really good — really good — at talking to people. That’s most of the game. If people are intrigued by you, they won’t lead off with “what’s your color” or “what’s your religion?” They will listen, because they want stuff to get fixed. People are desperate to have someone talk to them intelligently.

I find myself, like you, very drawn to him. Part of it is he’s very handsome — maybe he would be the most handsome president since Kennedy.

He really does. And then the way he communicates is very intelligent and like you said, compelling.

So you got the whole package. I mean, whoever says in politics that looks are a bad thing? If you’re blessed with looks, you’re way ahead of the game. You’re standing up there and people are looking at you. And then if God knows you can combine it with language, it’s potent. But this guy’s smart. That’s why I like him. I don’t feel insulted when he talks to me. I don’t feel he’s talking to me in cliches.

There is a war going on in your book between the young and the old. The young resent the old to the point of wanting to harm them.

If you go look at Europe now, you look at France, that revolution is on the ground. I am telling you it’s coming here. Because at some point, I don’t care how intelligent the politician is, I don’t think there’s an ability to solve the world’s money issues without many millions of people getting screwed.

It’s funny, all the discoveries now with AI, it’s all about, “Oh my God, maybe people could live to be 120.” And I have to laugh — because 25-year-olds don’t want to take care of 75-year-olds. You think they’re going to want to take care of 125-year-olds? “Hey, Bobby, I got some news for you! Because Grandpa can now live an extra 50 years, you’re going to have to work two more hours a week.”

What does a 25-year-old today have to look forward to compared with a 25-year-old a generation ago?

Right now, if you’re 25, you are guaranteed much less than when your father or your grandfather was 25, because they had the possibility of long employment. You could get a job for 30 years, you would get a pension, you would get a guarantee of healthcare, and that was your life. That’s how you built your foundation.

That’s all gone. I don’t know of anybody in their 20s that are looking for lifetime work. It’s gig to gig to gig. And what does that do? That makes healthcare really difficult.

All we’re doing in my perception is we’re delaying the inevitable and hoping that something called AI will fix it. But in fact, AI is more likely to because more of it because no one has explained to me when all the robots are here, what people are going to be doing. “Hey, is this Bob? Bob, this is United Industries. Do you want to clean the robot’s wheels?” “Yes. What does that pay?” “Oh, not a lot, Bob. Like $20 a wheel.”

Remember that guy Andrew Yang who ran on universal basic income? Well, what does that even mean? “Hey, Seth, no more work, but relax. What do you got? 50 years left? I’ll give you 40 grand a year. Have fun, baby.” Because in my mind, you’d have to raise an entire population from zero to teach them how to live in that world. The people that are alive today don’t know how to sit for the rest of their lives and do nothing. It’s just not how we’re programmed.

Now the thing that hasn’t come true in the book, but will, hopefully not in my lifetime, is the “Big One” earthquake I talk about. An event so over the top that the country couldn’t respond.

Reading about the L.A. earthquake in your book, I couldn’t help thinking of the fires in Pacific Palisades and Altadena.

And by the way, nothing is being done at a rate that anyone hoped for. I drove by there. There are some houses being rebuilt. This thing’s going to take a decade, minimum. We don’t do things quickly. That’s just the way it is. So that’s why in the book, when China offers to take half of the land in exchange for rebuilding, it was very appealing to the United States. Because God knows they build quickly.

I wrote this in 2010, published in 2011, and we’re what, about 15 years later, and this stuff looks more real to me today than it did when I wrote it.

Some of the other things you get right: You describe a Dick Tracy-style futuristic watch that sounds a lot like the Apple Watch.

And cars you get into and tell where to go.

Right. I also suggest health kiosks around a city. You would be diagnosed electronically, and then if it was more serious, you’d go to the hospital. These kiosks, I think, is something that will happen.

Well, you’re leaving something out though, which is that you give one drop of blood and it analyzes it and tells you what’s wrong with you. What does that remind me of?

Yes, Theranos. Right. Well, in my book, it worked.

I’ve been sensing this for many, many years. I didn’t write the book just by getting up one day. I wrote the book because I thought this is what I feel and I don’t know how else to express it. I would never have gotten a budget to make a movie this big, so I had to write it.

That’s my next question. So you did the great take on heaven in Defending Your Life. Would you do a futuristic film?

Well, the thing is, I presented this as a series and wrote with a friend of mine about four episodes. And right before COVID, FX bought it.

That’s right. But then sitting dead for three years where nobody was doing anything, it didn’t survive. And I feel bad about that. They committed to Shogun. Every day I watch programs on television and in my heart, I think this is still the big story. Until people can see it, I don’t think they comprehend it.

And that’s another thing you say in the book, that there’s no more legacy news outlets that you can trust. Everything is just splintered into a million pieces and you have to make up your own mind — which is where we live now, no?

Absolutely. I had this discussion the other day to someone just about truth and I said, “What is truth?” When something, a human event, happens, it’s real — and then forever it’s reflected and it’s talked about. And the more time goes by, the more the truth is completely gone.

But I’m telling you — this Ossoff made me go, “Holy moly, holy moly. Maybe my antenna was really working.”

So let’s get you on the record. You think Jon Ossoff is going to be president?

I do. I don’t know if it’ll be ’28 or ’32, but we’ll see how he does in the Senate. Let me just say this. I haven’t seen a person who so many people that I run into say, “Oh boy.” I’m just looking for someone who can help — who can undo some of the craziness because no candidate’s going to be able to snap their fingers and fix everything.

#708. Teddy Swims’ ‘Mr. Know It All’ Hits No. 1 on Billboard Pop Airplay Chart

The singer-songwriter scores his second leader at the format, after "Lose Control" in 2024.

Teddy Swims earns his second No. 1 on Billboard’s Pop Airplay chart as “Mr. Know It All” ascends two spots to the top of the Nov. 14-dated ranking.

Released on SWIMS Int./Warner Records, the song becomes the singer-songwriter’s second leader at the format, after “Lose Control” reigned for two weeks in April 2024.

The Pop Airplay chart measures songs’ weekly plays, as tabulated by Mediabase and provided to Billboard by Luminate, on nearly 150 U.S. mainstream top 40 radio stations.

Swims has also hit the Pop Airplay top 10 with “Bad Dreams,” which reached No. 8 in April 2025, and “The Door” (No. 9, November 2024).

On the all-genre, multimetric Billboard Hot 100, “Mr. Know It All,” which Swims cowrote, has hit a No. 26 high, likewise becoming Swims’ fourth top 40 hit, after “Bad Dreams” (No. 30), “The Door” (No. 24) and “Lose Control” (No. 1 for one week). “Lose Control” went on to rule as the No. 1 song on the 2024 year-end Hot 100.

“I feel like every time I meet one, I’m grateful, but I’m never satisfied,” Swims told Billboard News’ Tetris Kelly earlier this year of how he assesses goals. “The human eye sees, like, 20 miles ahead, right? So soon as you get that 20 miles, you’re seeing 20 more miles and you’re, like, there’s still much further to go. So I always try to celebrate the wins, but I want to be the best. I try to just be where my feet are and know that this is where I’m supposed to be.”

Added the father of a now-16-month-old, “I just also want my son to think I’m cool.”

All charts dated Nov. 14 will update Tuesday, Nov. 10, on Billboard.com.

Two spacewalking astronauts will finish upgrading the International Space Station's power system today (Nov. 5), and you can watch the action live.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and the Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk will install the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) today, during a roughly seven-hour spacewalk that's scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA, beginning at 7 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT).

Today's extravehicular activity (EVA) will be the second in a week for Menon and Kutryk, who installed the station's seventh iROSA during an Oct. 29 spacewalk. That excursion was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the ISS to date, and the first EVA for a Canadian astronaut since 2019.

Today's spacewalk will wrap up an ambitious ISS power upgrade that has taken more than five years to pull off.

"The installation job will complete the years-long process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts," NASA officials wrote about the EVA in a blog post on Tuesday (Nov. 3). That's a boost of about 30%.

Menon and Kutryk are currently sharing the ISS with five other astronauts — NASA's Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Delaney, Kutryk, Teteryatnikov and Watkins arrived at the ISS on Oct. 1, on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission. Dubrov, Kikina and Menon got there in mid-July, aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

#706. Fox Agrees to Keep Roku Open to Rivals in Justice Department Greenlight

The deal gives Fox control over a platform that's the gateway to content for millions of households.

The Justice Department’s clearance of Fox Corp.’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku is coming with concessions.

As part of its agreement with the competition regulators, Fox said it would remain open to rivals, according to the Justice Department. The company will continue carrying non-Fox movies and TV shows for at least three years, ensure competing services aren’t pushed down in search results or denied prominent placement on home screens and make audience data available to third parties. It also agreed to maintain safeguards preventing it from sharing sensitive information about rival content providers, including data on what users search for, watch and click until at least 2029.

Fox on Friday closed the deal, creating a new power player in media and streaming. The deal catapults the company into a major player, with two of the largest free streaming video platforms in Tubi and Roku and a premium streaming service in Fox One. And through Roku, it gains control of a behemoth distribution platform through which millions of households access TV, including applications operated by competitors like Netflix, YouTube and Disney+.

In its investigation, the Justice Department concluded that the deal is “not likely to result in harm to competition” in free, ad-supported streaming.

“Additionally, the investigation found that, because Roku relies on a broad offering of content from many providers to attract consumers, the merged firm would suffer monetary and reputational harm if it attempted to use the Roku platform to harm FOX’s content rivals,” the Justice Department said.

The transaction gives Fox major sway over how audiences discover and access content. Roku’s operating system powers its own streaming devices and is built into TVs. Its home screen is the gateway to those services for a significant chunk of the United States: Viewers use it to find apps, search for programming and, perhaps most important, decide what to watch.

The megamerger has been more than a year in the making, though the deal closed in just five months.

#705. In Canada: Faouzia to Accept the Breakthrough Award at Billboard Canada Women in Music 2026

Also up north this week: Angine de Poitrine reveals a third member at a Toronto concert and SOCAN joins GEMA's live music royalty network.

Faouzia‘s music is taking off in a big way, and the Moroccan-Canadian artist is about to receive a major honour in recognition of that momentum: the Breakthrough Award Presented by FACTOR at Billboard Canada Women In Music 2026.

The singer, born Faouzia Ouihya, debuted on the Billboard Canadian Hot 100 two months ago with “Unethical,” a single that dropped over a year ago and has gone viral in a big way.

“Unethical” became the singer’s first song to receive over a million Spotify daily streams in September, which Faouzia said she was “forever grateful” for. The song has reached 150 million global streams and become her second most-streamed single. It continues to climb the charts, with a new peak in each of its eight weeks on the chart. It is also climbing the Billboard Global 200 with streaming momentum in countries including the U.K., South Africa, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, UAE and more.

The song is reportedly inspired by an ultimatum Faouzia received from an ex who asked her to prioritize their relationship over her singing career. Her virtuosic vocal delivery and emotion have turned it into a viral TikTok clip, with “Unethical” live performance clips circling across social media. Some fans have even tried their hand at singing the song. The official “Unethical” sound plays in over 44,000 Instagram Reels and over 533,000 TikTok posts.

The orchestral pop ballad was one of the first tastes of her debut album, Film Noir, released in 2025, followed by a deluxe edition in June. Following its release, it received much acclaim, with Faouzia now sitting at over 10 million monthly listeners on Spotify. The project was followed by a highly anticipated deluxe version, Film Noir (fin), in June, with three additional tracks.

What makes the achievement even more impressive is that she’s done it as an independent artist. Two years ago, Faouzia announced that she was “now an independent artist for the first time in 6+ years” after parting ways with her former label, Atlantic Records/Warner Music Canada, where she released her first two EPs, Stripped and Citizens.

It’s been a slow and steady ascent for Faouzia that is now paying off. Faouzia has worked with some of the biggest acts across multiple genres, including David Guetta, Galantis, John Legend and Martin Solveig. She is even credited as a co-writer on Ye and Ty Dolla $ign’s “Beg Forgiveness,” released in 2024.

Faouzia will accept the Breakthrough Award Presented by FACTOR at this year’s third edition of Billboard Canada Women In Music, hosted by Leandra Earl and Kylie Miller of The Beaches. She’ll be honoured alongside the first-ever Global Woman of the Year, Cardi B, Global Hitmaker Bebe Rexha, Rising Star Chxrry, Global Visionary Summer Walker, Trailblazer Tia Wood, Innovator Blond:ish, Executive of the Year, Live Nation Canada’s Melissa Bubb-Clarke and Impact Award recipient, MusiCounts/The Juno Awards’ Kristy Fletcher.

Billboard Canada Women In Music 2026 will be held on Nov. 24 at Rebel in Toronto. Tickets are available here.

Angine de Poitrine have returned to Canada, and they didn’t come alone.

The viral Quebec math rock pair and Billboard Canada cover stars returned to Toronto last night (Nov. 5) to play a sold-out show at History and surprised the crowd with new music, and even a new member. Joining Khn and Klek de Poitrine onstage was a new polka-dotted alien with a cube-shaped head, a long nose similar to Khn’s and two horns in the shape of the signature yellow triangle featured on the group’s usual attire. He held up his triangle as the crowd cheered before one much-anticipated “ding” of the triangle.

Angine de Poitrine debuted an upbeat new track with a percussion break, during which their latest member delivered a high-energy (and somewhat tongue-in-cheek) triangle solo before clanging along with the original two members. It’s the second taste of new music the group have given fans in less than two months, after debuting the summery “Zugzegk” on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in September, a track whose title refers to the band’s wild “success” over the past year.

Their History show kicks off their latest North American run and marks their return to Toronto for the first time since their packed debut in the city in July, which included a trio of Mod Club shows and an opening stint for Jack White at RBC Amphitheatre and an appearance at FIFA Fan Fest. They also performed at the Polaris Music Prize gala. The band will play its two next dates on home turf, with a show at Quebec City’s Impérial Bell tonight (Nov. 6) and a return to Montreal’s Club Soda on Nov. 16 — the same venue where they launched their Billboard-charting breakthrough LP, Vol. II.

Their homecoming coincides with some major recent accolades, including a Polaris double win in September and four wins at the Premier Gala ADISQ this week (Nov. 4). After racking up a staggering 11 nominations, they are still vying for several of the top honours at the main ADISQ Gala (celebrating Quebec music), which takes place in Montreal on Sunday (Nov. 8).

SOCAN has joined GEMA’s live royalty network, One Arena.

The Canadian music rights society has become the first non-European rights collection company to join the initiative, which is meant to provide transparency surrounding live music and concert royalties. One Arena’s mission is to track concerts worldwide and provide information about licensing and royalty payments, giving a clearer picture of how performance royalties are calculated and distributed to musicians.

With SOCAN on board, One Arena will now add major Canadian concerts to its repertoire, while SOCAN will be able to access performance royalty information pertaining to other One Arena members and their international concerts. The network now counts eight members, with seven European organizations: SUISA (Switzerland & Liechtenstein), AKM (Austria), Buma-Stemra (Netherlands), KODA (Denmark), TONO (Norway), OSA (Czech Republic) and GEMA (Germany).

“One Arena’s strength lies in the expertise and commitment of all the collecting societies involved,” said Dr. Tobias Holzmüller, CEO of GEMA. “Together, we’re building greater transparency and making it easier for songwriters and artists to understand how royalties are generated by their international live performances. We’re delighted to welcome SOCAN into our network; this will enable us to draw on SOCAN’s expertise in the Canadian market and support even more rightsholders in the future through One Arena.”

The move comes amid a year of expansion and action for SOCAN, particularly defined by its acquisition of the CMRRA (Canadian Musical Reproduction Rights Agency) and its blockbuster copyright infringement lawsuit against Suno, in which the collection society sued the AI music generation application for over $10 million in September. A few months prior, the German court ruled in favour of GEMA after the German society filed its own copyright lawsuit against Suno for infringing on tracks in its database such as Boney M.’s “Rasputin” and Lou Bega’s “Mambo No. 5.”

“For songwriters, a concert doesn’t end with the final note. When it comes to international performances in particular, the path to collecting and distributing royalties is often long and has information gaps,” said Jennifer Brown, CEO of SOCAN. “One Arena helps us to track our members’ performances abroad more efficiently, with a level of transparency that is welcomed in the live performance sector. We’re delighted to be part of this network that is putting the needs and royalties of members first.”

Last year, performance royalties played a central role in the legal dispute between SOCAN and the Festival d’été de Québec (FEQ) in which the festival was sued for allegedly not having a license from SOCAN and failing to pay royalties to the society for three years. The claim was resolved by both parties at the beginning of this year.

#704. The Other Midterms Flip: Broadcast Networks, Led by NBC, Dominated Election Night Coverage

Broadcasters accounted for 57 percent of primetime viewing on Tuesday.

In addition to changing the composition of Congress and a number of statehouses, the midterm elections brought another kind of disruption to the status quo: For the first time in 6 election cycles, more people watched the returns come in on network TV than on cable.

Per Nielsen ratings, 31.21 million people watched primetime election coverage on 13 broadcast and cable outlets Tuesday, significantly more than the 25.43 million viewers for the 2022 midterms. Of that audience, 57 percent (17.79 million) watched on broadcast outlets (NBC, ABC, CBS, Univision, Telemundo and PBS), and just 43 percent (13.42 million) on cable channels. That’s exactly the inverse of four years ago, when 57 percent of viewers went to cable for midterm coverage.

It’s been 14 years since broadcast networks drew a clear majority of election night viewers (there was a roughly 50-50 split in 2016). That was also the last election a broadcaster led all comers on — and in both 2012 and this year, NBC finished first.

The network had 6.74 million viewers in primetime Tuesday, more than doubling its 2022 average. ABC also improved considerably, growing by 57 percent from four years ago to 5.19 million viewers. CBS was off the pace some at 2.76 million, but it also improved by 8 percent from 2022. Univision (1.54 million), Telemundo (1.06 million) and PBS (about 500,000) made up the rest of the broadcast total.

CNN and MS NOW also improved their numbers from 2022, but Fox News tumbled by almost 3.5 million viewers (though it still narrowly led its cable counterparts). The big three broadcasters, however, collectively gained more viewers than Fox News lost, so the off night for Fox doesn’t fully explain the shift in balance from cable to broadcast.

So what does? For one, cable as a whole has also suffered across-the-board declines in the past four years. Homes with multi-channel providers (cable, satellite or digital services like YouTube TV or Hulu + Live TV) only represent 42.5 percent of TV homes now, down from 52.3 percent four years ago. That represents a loss of more than 10 million households.

Some of it might also be ideological: Fox News leans right, and a night when Republicans took bruising losses might have helped drive ratings down there. MS NOW’s gains could similarly be put down to a blue wave helping the left-leaning channel.

Tuesday’s viewer leaders, ABC and NBC, work to project big-tent inclusiveness, which seems to have paid off some. Marc Greenstein, executive vp creative production and field operations for NBC News, pointed to reporting initiatives on the NBC Nightly News and Meet the Press that try go beyond the “left-right food fight,” as he put it, and explore substantive issues and points of commonality.

NBC also scored a multi-platform win Tuesday, as its dedicated “Kornacki Cam” live stream of analyst Steve Kornacki throughout the night was the most watched live stream of election coverage. NBC News as a whole led election night streams with 4.39 million hours of viewing on its YouTube channels, according to analytics firm Streams Charts (Twitch streamer Hasan Piker was second with 1.75 million hours).

The Kornacki Cam was also something of a tech breakthrough for NBC News, Greenstein said. Kornacki was stationed about 15 feet away from the network’s main desk, but both the TV broadcast and the live stream were able to run simultaneously without interfering with one another. NBC used software from a company called Waves that filters audio, allowing for clean sound on both despite their proximity.

“I talked to our engineering team maybe a week and a half before the elections, and it just so happened that [Saturday Night Live] had just started using it not too long before,” Greenstein said. “We were literally in the midst of rehearsals when we turned this thing on, and we decided to take the risk and put it out there because we thought it was much more important to really integrate Steve into the [TV] broadcast.”

The live stream and on-air telecast ended up being mutually reinforcing, Greenstein said, possibly helping draw viewers in. NBC’s decision desk was also among the fastest to call some key races and the first to project Democratic control of the U.S. Senate.

That said, Greeenstein didn’t know ahead of Tuesday night that NBC would end up at the top of the ratings.

“We like to think we put in really good groundwork and incredible preparation going into the night, so we always hope that the audience will pay us back for that work,” Greenstein told The Hollywood Reporter. “One thing I will say is that I think NBC, maybe more than others, we just do big events well as a network. You look at the Super Bowl, the Olympics, election night — we just have a bigness and a gravitas. I think that matters on these type of nights, and I think that is an advantage we have.”

#700. Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO

Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.

The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility, each more than 500 meters (1,640 feet) long, look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles), allowing Russia to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.

The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," Malinionis added.

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals, citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.

"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.

"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.

"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE defense company sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.

"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.

The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.

"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."

Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.

The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

#699. Paul Howard, Son of Moe Howard of The Three Stooges, Dies at 91

He connected with fans of the iconic comedy act at conventions and hosted a nine-part 2015 docuseries called ‘Hey Moe, Hey Dad!’

Paul Howard, the only son of Moe Howard of The Three Stooges and the narrator of a nine-part 2015 docuseries about the legendary American comedy team, has died. He was 91.

Howard lived on Upper East Side of Manhattan and died this week, a spokesperson for C3 Entertainment, the owner of The Three Stooges license and brand, announced. He was the last remaining son of the original comedy team that consisted of Moe, his brothers Curly and Shemp and Larry Fine.

Since Moe’s death in 1975 at age 77, Paul Howard served as a guardian of his father’s legacy, offering fans a unique, firsthand view of the man behind the iconic bowl-cut hairdo and timeless slapstick comedy. Related Stories Movies Helene Hahn Loyd, Former Disney and DreamWorks SKG Exec, Dies at 78 TV Kimmarie Johnson, 'Beverly Hills, 90210' Actress, Dies at 50

He connected with generations of the Stooges faithful at conventions and events over the decades, sharing stories, memories and insights into the lives of his dad, his Uncle Shemp and his Uncle Curly.

The docuseries Hey Moe, Hey Dad! features rare archival footage, personal family accounts and interviews with members of the Howard, Fine and DeRita families (Curly Joe DeRita was another member of the Stooges act) and fans including Whoopi Goldberg and Leonard Maltin. (The series is available on The Three Stooges+ YouTube channel.)

Moe married Helen Schonberger — a cousin of famed escape artist Harry Houdini — in June 1925, and they welcomed their first child, Joan, in April 1927. Paul arrived on July 8, 1935. (Helen died six months after Moe did, and Joan, a writer and actress, died in September 2021 at age 94.

Paul lived in Rifton, New York, for more than 40 years before relocating to Manhattan. His survivors include his wife, Joanne; his daughter, Jennifer; his nephew, Jeffrey; and a cousin, Janie Howard Hanky, daughter of Curly (she was born in May 1948).
